meta.name: AST SpaceMobile, Inc.
meta.title: AST SpaceMobile — Abel Avellan's direct-to-cell satellite network through the BlueBird constellation
meta.subtitle: From the 2017 Midland-Texas founding through the 2021 SPAC listing into the BlueBird operational deployment that targets satellite-to-standard-smartphone connectivity at global scale
meta.abstract: AST SpaceMobile, Inc. (ASTS, NASDAQ) is the Midland, Texas-headquartered direct-to-cell satellite operator developing the SpaceMobile network — a low Earth orbit satellite constellation designed to provide cellular broadband service directly to standard unmodified mobile phones in partnership with terrestrial mobile network operators globally. The company was founded in 2017 by Abel Avellan, the Venezuelan-born telecommunications and satellite industry executive who previously founded Emerging Markets Communications and held senior roles at Hughes Electronics and Astrolink. AST SpaceMobile went public via SPAC business combination with New Providence Acquisition Corp in April 2021. Avellan continues as Chairman of the Board and CEO; CFO Andrew Johnson, Chief Strategy Officer Sean Wallace, and the broader executive team support the multi-year capital-intensive constellation deployment programme. The strategic differentiation is structural — AST SpaceMobile is one of only two meaningful commercial direct-to-cell satellite operators (the other being SpaceX Starlink's emerging direct-to-cell service through partnership with T-Mobile). The five operational BlueBird satellites launched in September 2024 demonstrated the direct-to-cell capability at commercial scale; subsequent Block 2 BlueBird satellites at substantially larger antenna scale (approximately 64 square metres of phased array antenna per satellite) are intended to deploy through 2026-2027 to establish broader commercial coverage. The mobile network operator partnership base includes AT&T (US), Verizon (US), Vodafone (multi-country), Rakuten (Japan), Bell Canada, Telefonica (multi-country), and Orange (multi-country) — covering an addressable subscriber base in the billions globally. Fiscal year 2025 (calendar year 2025) revenue was minimal as the company remains substantially pre-commercial; the FY2025 net loss was substantial reflecting the constellation deployment capex plus broader R&D investment. The cash position at year-end 2025 was substantial reflecting multiple equity issuances supporting the multi-year deployment. The investment proposition compresses the constellation deployment execution timeline, the commercial revenue scaling once Block 2 satellites reach operational coverage, the mobile network operator partnership monetisation, and the competitive dynamics versus SpaceX Starlink's direct-to-cell service plus emerging satellite-to-handset alternatives.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On 12 September 2024, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Cape Canaveral carrying five BlueBird satellites — the first operational nodes of AST SpaceMobile's planned global direct-to-cell constellation. The launch marked a hard boundary in the company's history, ending a seven-year development phase and placing AST SpaceMobile (ticker: ASTS, NASDAQ) into early operational status. Founder, Chairman, and Chief Executive Abel Avellan had built the company from its 2017 Midland, Texas origins around a single structural bet: that a satellite constellation deploying large, unfolded phased-array antennas in low Earth orbit could connect standard, unmodified smartphones — via existing LTE 4G and 5G bands — without any new hardware on the ground. By the September 2024 launch, that bet had drawn in ~~AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone~~ ==AT&T, Vodafone==, Rakuten Mobile, Bell Canada, Telstra, MTN, and more than fifty mobile network operators collectively covering roughly three billion subscribers across the globe. ==Verizon's definitive commercial agreement followed on 8 October 2025.==

## The Architecture of the Founding Thesis

AST SpaceMobile's proposition to mobile operators was structurally distinct from prior satellite-to-phone ventures. Rather than a bespoke handset or a proprietary spectrum layer, Avellan's design positioned the satellite as a roaming cell tower in orbit — one that hands off to and from terrestrial networks, uses the MNO's licensed spectrum, and bills through the existing operator relationship. Execution required antennas of a scale not previously deployed commercially in low Earth orbit. The BlueWalker 3 prototype, launched in September 2022, demonstrated the concept: direct-to-handset voice and broadband data at commercially relevant speeds from a single large unfolded array. The prototype's success — and the FCC Supplemental Coverage from Space approvals that followed — validated the core engineering thesis and unlocked the commercial framework with U.S. partners.

The company reached the public markets on 7 April 2021 through a SPAC merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp. The listing provided initial capital and public-company currency, though the intervening three years from listing to the first BlueBird launch were consumed by satellite design, antenna engineering, manufacturing scale-up, and the iterative regulatory work required across more than fifty national jurisdictions. Throughout, Avellan maintained a triple-role structure — Chairman, CEO, and President — characteristic of founder-controlled capital-intensive programmes.

## BlueBird Constellation: Block 1 and the First Block 2 Node

The five BlueBird Block 1 satellites launched in September 2024 completed antenna deployment by late October 2024. No further Block 1 units followed. The production programme had already pivoted to the substantially more capable Block 2 design — approximately 3.5 times the antenna area of Block 1, with a peak data throughput of 120 Mbps per satellite against Block 1's narrower baseline, and roughly 10x the data capacity per node. The first Block 2 unit, BlueBird 6, launched 23 December 2025 aboard an ISRO LVM3 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre — the heaviest commercial LEO payload the Indian rocket had ever carried, at approximately 6,100 kilograms, with an antenna array spanning nearly 2,400 square feet and described by the company as the largest commercial communications array deployed in LEO. [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ast-spacemobile-raises-400-million-to-accelerate-direct-to-smartphone-plans/); [SatNews](https://satnews.com/2025/12/24/ast-spacemobile-deploys-bluebird-6-largest-commercial-array-in-leo/).

A second Block 2 satellite, BlueBird 7, was lost on 19 April 2026 following an anomaly on a Blue Origin New Glenn second stage that left the spacecraft in an unsustainable orbit. AST SpaceMobile initiated a controlled deorbit and recorded an estimated write-off of $155–$160 million in the second quarter of 2026. As of the 23 May 2026 snapshot date, six BlueBirds were operational in orbit: the five Block 1 units and BlueBird 6. [Aviation Week](https://aviationweek.com/space/launch-vehicles-propulsion/ast-spacemobile-declares-satellite-lost-after-new-glenn-launch).

## Revenue, Capital, and the MNO Partnership Stack

Revenue through the snapshot date remained pre-commercial in the consumer-service sense. Full-year 2025 revenue of $70.9 million — and $14.7 million in the first quarter of 2026 — derived principally from gateway hardware deliveries and government programme milestones rather than subscriber-level mobile service billings. [Q1 2026 results via StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/ASTS/8-k-ast-space-mobile-inc-reports-material-event-75ced08d18a6.html). The company had assembled a contracted minimum revenue backlog exceeding $1.2 billion, anchored by commitments including a $175 million prepayment from Saudi Telecom Group and a $45 million contingent commercial payment from Verizon. [Q4 2025 transcript via Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/03/02/ast-spacemobile-asts-q4-2025-earnings-transcript/).

Capital structure reflected the demands of a multi-year pre-revenue constellation deployment. Strategic equity from Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, and Google ==— AT&T and Google entering through the January 2024 strategic investment —== provided both validation and non-dilutive partnership anchor. Successive convertible note issuances — $460 million in January 2025, $575 million in July 2025, and $1.0 billion in February 2026 — together with an active at-the-market equity programme, built a cash position of approximately $3.5 billion as of 31 March 2026. [Business Wire, $1B notes Feb 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260211283238/en/AST-SpaceMobile-Announces-Proposed-Private-Offering-of-%241.0-Billion-of-Convertible-Senior-Notes-Due-2036). Capital commitments against that balance included roughly $383 million for satellite procurement and $145–175 million for launch contracts.

## The Competitive Frame

The primary commercial reference point had shifted materially by mid-2025. SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell service, partnered with T-Mobile as "T-Satellite," commercially launched text messaging and selective data connectivity on 23 July 2025, with voice following in late beta. [Broadband Breakfast](https://broadbandbreakfast.com/t-mobile-and-starlink-satellite-service-to-officially-launch-july-23/). By the snapshot date, Starlink operated more than 650 direct-to-cell satellites with FCC approval for 7,500 additional nodes — a constellation scale that gave it a structural head start in commercial activation, though at substantially lower per-satellite bandwidth capacity than AST's Block 2 design targets. AST's commercial service remained contingent on reaching an operational threshold of approximately 25 to 45 satellites, which management guided for the second half of 2026.

---

This dossier proceeds from that posture. The core analytical questions are four: whether Block 2 satellite production and launch execution can reach the constellation threshold necessary for commercial service activation; whether the contracted MNO partnerships translate into the subscriber revenue required to justify the capital structure; how the Starlink Direct to Cell commercial head start shapes operator partnership decisions and consumer adoption sequencing; and whether the approximately $3.5 billion cash position — against quarterly net losses approaching $190 million and substantial remaining capex obligations — is sufficient to carry the programme to self-funding commercial scale without further significant dilution.

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through BlueWalker 3, SPAC, and BlueBird operational launches
chapters.body:
## Midland Origins: The Founding Thesis

Abel Avellan arrived at the founding idea for AST SpaceMobile in 2017 carrying a specific kind of operational scar tissue. The Venezuelan-born telecommunications entrepreneur had spent the preceding decade building Emerging Markets Communications — a satellite connectivity business that threaded broadband service into maritime vessels, remote oil rigs, and underserved communities across the developing world. When Global Eagle Entertainment acquired EMC in 2016 for approximately $550 million, Avellan left with both the proceeds and a clarifying conviction: the gap between satellite capacity and the ordinary mobile handset in a person's pocket remained unbridged by design, and that gap was large enough to build a company around closing.

He established AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas — an energy-industry town whose infrastructure and landlord economics suited an early-stage hardware business better than the coastal aerospace corridors around Los Angeles or northern Virginia. The founding thesis was precise: engineer a low Earth orbit satellite carrying a phased-array antenna large enough to communicate directly with standard, unmodified smartphones on the cellular spectrum bands that mobile network operators already licensed and their customers already used. No special handset. No proprietary terminal. The service would arrive over existing LTE and eventually 5G NR air interfaces, delivered from orbit at roughly 500 kilometres altitude, and sold to consumers through the MNO partner rather than directly. The satellite network would function as a seamless extension of the terrestrial mobile network — invisible infrastructure extending coverage into the roughly 85 percent of the Earth's surface that ground-based towers did not reach.

The engineering challenge embedded in that thesis was formidable. Communicating directly with a handset from LEO required concentrating enough signal through an antenna surface area orders of magnitude larger than any satellite the industry had previously attempted in that orbit. Avellan's engineering team set to work on a foldable phased-array design that could be stowed inside a rocket fairing and then unfurl in orbit to dimensions previously associated with large GEO communications platforms rather than nimble LEO craft. The technical credibility of the approach — or the lack of it — would define how much capital the company could attract before flight hardware validated the physics.

## Early Capital and the MNO Partnership Architecture

Before the company could access public capital markets, Avellan built the strategic investor base that would later differentiate AST SpaceMobile's commercial architecture from hardware-only satellite competitors. Vodafone Group took an equity stake, as did Rakuten Mobile — the Japanese carrier that had staked its 4G network build-out on virtualised, open-architecture radio infrastructure and had a particular interest in inexpensive coverage extension. Both operators saw in AST SpaceMobile the prospect of expanding their network footprints without the capital intensity of terrestrial tower densification in hard terrain. Their investment was strategic rather than purely financial: they contributed cellular-spectrum access rights and MNO ecosystem credibility alongside cash.

The partnership model that crystallised from those early relationships established the commercial template the company would carry through listing and into operations. Rather than licensing spectrum independently or selling handsets, AST SpaceMobile would operate the satellite network on behalf of MNO partners who retained the subscriber relationship and billing infrastructure. Engineering-services revenue from the pre-commercial partnership arrangements provided a modest income stream — ~~$11 million in 2022 and $12 million in 2023~~ ==approximately $11 million in 2022, with no GAAP revenue recognised in 2023,== per the company's SEC filings — during the constellation-development phase, though this was insufficient to cover substantial operating losses accumulating across the satellite-manufacturing programme.

~~AT&T subsequently signed a multi-year commercial agreement, as did Verizon — a competitive pairing that gave AST SpaceMobile bilateral coverage of the US carrier market and the implicit endorsement of the two largest American mobile operators.~~ ==The definitive US-carrier commercial agreements would arrive much later, well after the public listing: AT&T on May 15, 2024 and Verizon on October 8, 2025, both after on-orbit demonstration of the direct-to-cell interface. The pairing would eventually give AST SpaceMobile bilateral coverage of the US carrier market and the implicit endorsement of the two largest American mobile operators.== Bell Canada, Telstra in Australia, and MTN across Africa expanded the roster, with the MNO partnership portfolio eventually spanning more than fifty countries. ~~Google also took an equity position, adding a major technology-sector endorsement to a pre-operational company whose satellite constellation existed, as of 2020, principally in engineering drawings and test hardware.~~ ==The pre-operational company's satellite constellation existed, as of 2020, principally in engineering drawings and test hardware. Google's equity participation arrived later, in the January 2024 strategic financing round alongside AT&T's strategic investment, not as part of the pre-listing investor base.==

## The April 2021 SPAC Merger

Access to public-market capital arrived on [April 7, 2021](https://investors.ast-science.com), when AST SpaceMobile completed its merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp and began trading on the NASDAQ under the ticker ASTS. The transaction followed the SPAC wave that had swept the US capital markets through the pandemic period, providing the company with listed equity currency and the gross proceeds needed to advance satellite manufacturing toward the prototype phase.

The listing placed the founding thesis — and its execution risks — squarely in front of public investors. The company was pre-revenue in any commercial sense, carried significant operating losses, and required continued capital to fund constellation deployment. The key risk factors ran through a satellite programme that had not yet placed a single operational vehicle in orbit. Strategic equity investors ~~including Vodafone, Rakuten, and Google~~ ==— principally Vodafone and Rakuten —== were on the shareholder register, providing institutional validation ~~across both the telecom and technology sectors~~ ==from the carrier-partner side==, but commercial viability remained contingent on on-orbit demonstration of the direct-to-cell air interface. Avellan retained the Chairman, CEO, and President roles through the transaction, preserving the concentrated founder-leadership structure that had governed the company since Midland. The board composition reflected the partnership architecture directly: directors representing ~~AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, and Rakuten~~ ==Vodafone and Rakuten== sat alongside independent directors and Avellan as Chairman, aligning governance with the MNO relationships on which commercial revenue ultimately depended.

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Physics

The first critical technical test came on September 10, 2022, when a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted BlueWalker 3 — the company's full-scale prototype satellite — into low Earth orbit from Cape Canaveral. BlueWalker 3 carried a phased-array antenna spanning 693 square feet (approximately 64.5 square metres), making it one of the largest commercial antenna arrays deployed in LEO to that point. The satellite's principal purpose was demonstration: validate that the fundamental physics of direct-to-cell satellite communication over standard LTE bands worked in actual orbital conditions, not only in laboratory simulations.

The results that followed through late 2022 and into 2023 delivered the confirmation Avellan had staked the company upon. BlueWalker 3 successfully completed direct-to-cell voice calls and data sessions using standard unmodified handsets — connectivity demonstrations conducted in partnership with AT&T and Vodafone that the MNO partners publicly acknowledged. Subsequent testing achieved 5G NR (New Radio) data connections, extending the demonstrated capability beyond 4G LTE and establishing the satellite platform's compatibility with the industry's forward-looking radio standards.

BlueWalker 3 also surfaced a complication that had not featured prominently in pre-launch analysis: the satellite's large reflective surface made it one of the brightest objects visible to ground-based observatories in its orbital slot, drawing criticism from astronomers concerned about optical brightness degrading telescope observations and radio-frequency interference with existing allocations. The company engaged with the International Astronomical Union and committed to brightness-mitigation measures on subsequent BlueBird production satellites — an environmental-governance dimension that the broader NewSpace industry was beginning to absorb as both a regulatory and reputational cost of large-constellation deployment.

## BlueBird Block 1: Transition to Operations

Two years after BlueWalker 3's launch, the company crossed the threshold from prototype demonstration to operational deployment. On [September 12, 2024](https://investors.ast-science.com), a SpaceX Falcon 9 carried the first five BlueBird Block 1 satellites — AST SpaceMobile's commercial production design — into LEO from Kennedy Space Center. The launch marked the company's transition from pre-operational development to early operational status and represented the practical conversion of seven years of engineering effort into revenue-generating infrastructure.

BlueBird Block 1 incorporated the antenna and systems architecture validated by BlueWalker 3 in a satellite design optimised for production manufacturing and constellation scaling rather than single-unit demonstration. The five initial satellites enabled ~~limited commercial service testing~~ ==engineering and pre-commercial service testing== with MNO partners across the US and select international markets through the remainder of 2024. ~~Commercial availability remained partial~~ ==Subscriber-facing SpaceMobile Service had not yet begun==, with service coverage constrained by the small initial constellation size — five satellites providing intermittent rather than continuous coverage to any fixed ground location as they passed overhead in succession.

The operational ramp exposed the next execution question plainly: scaling from five early-commercial satellites to a constellation dense enough to offer continuous, commercially competitive coverage required both the Block 2 programme and sustained capital access. Block 2 satellites, designed with substantially larger antenna apertures — approximately two to three times the area of Block 1 units — would deliver higher per-satellite capacity and improved spectral efficiency, with deployment timelines extending into 2025 and 2026.

## Milestone Chronology

| Era | Date | Event |
|---|---|---|
| Founding | 2017 | AST SpaceMobile established, Midland, Texas |
| Strategic capital | 2018–2020 | ~~Vodafone, Rakuten, Google equity; MNO partnership framework~~ ==Vodafone and Rakuten equity; early MNO partnership framework== |
| Public listing | April 7, 2021 | SPAC merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp; NASDAQ: ASTS |
| Prototype launch | September 10, 2022 | BlueWalker 3 via SpaceX Falcon 9, Cape Canaveral |
| Direct-to-cell validation | 2022–2024 | LTE voice, 5G NR data demonstrated on unmodified handsets |
| ==Strategic investment== | ==January 2024== | ==Google and AT&T strategic financing round== |
| ==AT&T commercial agreement== | ==May 15, 2024== | ==Definitive multi-year direct-to-cell commercial agreement== |
| Operational launch | September 12, 2024 | BlueBird Block 1, first 5 commercial satellites via SpaceX Falcon 9 |
| ==Verizon commercial agreement== | ==October 8, 2025== | ==Definitive multi-year direct-to-cell commercial agreement== |

From Midland to operational orbit in seven years, Avellan's trajectory traced a line that most satellite-industry veterans had considered technically implausible at its inception. The BlueWalker 3 demonstration answered the physics question. The BlueBird Block 1 launch answered the manufacturing question. What remained — MNO commercial revenue conversion at scale and the Block 2 deployment programme — was the substance of the forward commercial chapters.

chapters.title: BlueBird satellites, MNO partnership model, single-product framework
chapters.body:
## A Single Product, Deployed Through Others

AST SpaceMobile was built around a conviction that many in the satellite industry treated as fanciful for years: that a satellite could close a link directly to an ordinary smartphone, with no special hardware on the ground, using the same LTE and 5G spectrum bands that terrestrial carriers had already licensed and deployed. The company's entire commercial architecture flowed from that proposition. From the time Abel Avellan incorporated AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas in 2017, through the April 2021 SPAC listing that gave it public-market capital, and into the September 2024 launch of its first operational satellites, the company offered exactly one product to the world: wholesale satellite connectivity, sold to mobile network operators, who would then extend it to their existing subscribers on existing handsets.

That product-market clarity was both a strength and a constraint. AST SpaceMobile held no retail relationships, collected no subscriber data directly, operated no billing infrastructure. What it possessed was the satellite constellation itself, the radio-access technology embedded within it, and the commercial agreements with the operators who held the last-mile relationships at scale. Its revenue, when it arrived, would be a share of what those operators generated from selling coverage to customers who happened to be outside terrestrial signal range.

## The Antenna That Made It Possible

The technology credibility problem AST SpaceMobile faced through its early years was fundamental. Closing a link from low-Earth orbit to a device with the transmit power, antenna gain, and form factor of a consumer handset required satellite antennas of unusual size. The physics were not flexible. A satellite operating at roughly 500 kilometers altitude communicating on cellular bands had to compensate for free-space path loss that dwarfs what a ground tower contends with. The engineering solution Avellan's team developed was the large unfoldable phased-array antenna panel — a structure that could be stowed compactly during launch and then deployed in orbit to dimensions far exceeding any conventional telecommunications satellite.

The BlueWalker 3 prototype, launched in September 2022 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 and into a 500-kilometer orbit, demonstrated the concept at scale for the first time. The satellite carried a 693-square-foot phased-array aperture — at the time of its deployment the largest commercial communications antenna ever operated in LEO. Over the following months it established direct voice calls and broadband data sessions with standard unmodified smartphones, completing a series of milestones the company had told investors to expect but that many in the industry had watched skeptically. The tests used existing cellular spectrum bands, required no firmware changes on the handsets involved, and were conducted in partnership with mobile operators whose spectrum licenses the satellite was operating within.

BlueWalker 3 was never intended for commercial service. Its role was validation: of the antenna structure, the phased-array electronics, the thermal management systems, the link budget assumptions that underpinned the entire business case. When the data came back from those tests, AST SpaceMobile's engineering program shifted toward productizing the design into a form that could be manufactured and launched at the scale the constellation required.

## BlueBird Block 1: The Operational Satellite

The first five operational BlueBird satellites lifted off on September 12, 2024, again on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral. The satellites constituted what AST SpaceMobile designated Block 1 — the initial production design, incorporating the lessons of BlueWalker 3 into a unit optimized for manufacturability and orbital deployment.

Block 1 satellites retained the core phased-array architecture. Each carried an antenna panel calibrated to provide broadband direct-to-cell coverage across a cellular footprint stretching hundreds of kilometers in diameter, sufficient to cover terrestrial dead zones — rural corridors, maritime approaches, remote terrain — that operators had accepted as uneconomic to cover with towers. The satellites operated in partnership with the spectrum holdings of AST SpaceMobile's MNO partners, using their licensed LTE and 5G frequencies rather than satellite-specific allocations, which was central to the seamless handset experience the product promised.

The September 2024 launch represented a transition from development-stage to early operational status. Five satellites were insufficient for continuous global coverage but sufficient to begin commercial service trials with the carriers that had signed multi-year agreements, and to generate the first data on operational performance at scale — satellite health, link quality across different geographies and atmospheric conditions, handoff behavior, and the performance consistency that carriers would need to validate before configuring their networks to route traffic through AST SpaceMobile's orbital layer.

## Block 2: Scaling Capacity

The Block 2 satellite design, in development for deployment during 2025 and 2026, represented a substantive step up in capability rather than an incremental refinement. AST SpaceMobile disclosed that Block 2 satellites would carry antenna apertures approximately two to three times the size of Block 1, with a proportional increase in per-satellite capacity. ==The Block 2 / BlueBird 6 generation, not Block 1, represented the principal aperture step-up beyond the BlueWalker 3 prototype's 693-square-foot panel.==

The significance of that scaling was commercial as much as technical. Constellation economics in direct-to-cell are driven by the capacity each satellite can deliver over a given coverage area, and larger apertures translate directly into more simultaneous user sessions, higher aggregate throughput, and better spectral efficiency within each carrier's licensed band. A Block 2 satellite serving the same orbital slot as a Block 1 unit could, in principle, support a meaningfully larger population of connected subscribers during its pass — compressing the number of satellites needed to reach any given service level, and improving the unit economics of the network per dollar of capital invested.

The transition from Block 1 to Block 2 deployment was therefore the principal scaling event in AST SpaceMobile's forward operational strategy as of the frozen snapshot date. Block 1 established that the system worked in commercial operation; Block 2 was designed to make it work at the throughput volumes that would matter to large carriers managing millions of subscriber minutes.

## The MNO Partnership Model

The commercial architecture AST SpaceMobile constructed around its technology was deliberately indirect. The company sought no direct relationships with the subscribers who would ultimately use its service. Instead, it executed commercial agreements with mobile network operators, under which the operator would market satellite coverage as an extension of its existing plans — and would pay AST SpaceMobile a share of the revenue those customers generated while connected through the satellite layer.

The appeal to operators was coverage without the capital expenditure of tower build-out. Terrestrial network densification in rural or remote areas had long been challenged by the economics of per-subscriber returns against cell tower construction and maintenance costs. AST SpaceMobile offered an alternative: operators could extend their coverage footprints to geographies they had never covered, using a wholesale arrangement that aligned AST SpaceMobile's revenue to actual traffic rather than requiring operators to pay fixed capacity fees regardless of demand.

By the time the BlueBird Block 1 satellites were in orbit, AST SpaceMobile had assembled a partner roster that reached across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Africa. In the United States, ~~both AT&T and Verizon held multi-year commercial agreements~~ ==AT&T held a definitive multi-year commercial agreement announced May 15, 2024; Verizon's definitive commercial agreement was not announced until October 8, 2025, more than a year after the Block 1 launch==. Internationally, Vodafone — which also held an equity stake in AST SpaceMobile — provided access to its multi-country European and African networks. Rakuten Mobile in Japan, similarly both a commercial partner and equity holder, represented a strategically significant relationship in a market where spectrum and regulatory access had historically been difficult for foreign satellite operators to secure.

Beyond those anchor names, AST SpaceMobile had signed agreements with Bell Canada, Telstra in Australia, and MTN across its African operations, with the total partner base reaching into more than fifty countries as of the snapshot date. The breadth of that partner list was significant not merely as a commercial milestone but as a demonstration that the MNO revenue-share model was replicable across regulatory jurisdictions — that AST SpaceMobile's approach to spectrum access and commercial arrangement could be reproduced carrier by carrier without requiring bespoke legal or technical engineering in every market.

| Partner | Geography | Equity Holder |
|---|---|---|
| AT&T | United States | No |
| Verizon | United States | No |
| Vodafone | Europe, Africa (multi-country) | Yes |
| Rakuten Mobile | Japan | Yes |
| Bell Canada | Canada | No |
| Telstra | Australia | No |
| MTN | Africa (multi-country) | No |

The equity stakes held by Vodafone and Rakuten were not incidental. They reflected the depth of strategic alignment those partners had made with AST SpaceMobile's trajectory — a financial bet on the technology alongside the commercial one, which carried different implications for the durability of the commercial relationships than a standard wholesale agreement might.

## What the Framework Excludes

The single-product model ~~defined~~ ==had defined== the company as sharply by what it chose not to do as by what it built. AST SpaceMobile held no consumer brand, operated no app or subscriber management platform, engaged in no device sales or direct marketing. It collected no revenue from IoT applications, ~~no government connectivity contracts in its own name,~~ no broadband resale to enterprise accounts. ==By the Q1 2026 reporting period, however, the revenue mix had begun to broaden modestly: gateway equipment generated product revenue alongside emerging service revenue, and SEC filings disclosed U.S. Government revenue and related performance obligations — narrowing, but not eliminating, the single-channel framing.== The strategic wager was that the direct-to-cell MNO partnership channel was large enough — and the wholesale value proposition compelling enough — that horizontal diversification would dilute rather than strengthen the commercial focus at a moment when execution on a single, technically demanding product remained the priority.

That bet would be tested as BlueBird Block 2 deployment proceeded and ~~the first full revenue cycles from AT&T and Verizon agreements moved from service trials toward commercial volume~~ ==the AT&T and Verizon agreements moved from the limited, noncontinuous SpaceMobile Service initiation described in the Q1 2026 10-Q toward commercial scale==.

chapters.title: Pre-commercial revenue, capital raises, and the constellation deployment economics
chapters.body:
## Engineering services and the revenue paradox of early deployment

By any conventional measure, AST SpaceMobile's top line through 2022 and 2023 was modest to the point of near-invisibility relative to the capital it was consuming. The company recorded approximately $11 million in revenue for 2022 ~~and $12 million in 2023, figures~~ ==— a figure== that reflected almost entirely engineering services billings and pre-commercial contributions from its mobile network operator partners — not a single dollar of recurring cellular connectivity revenue. ==2023 GAAP revenue then printed at zero as those bilateral development billings rolled off entirely.== Then, in a twist that illustrated the peculiar accounting geography of a company transitioning from prototype to deployment, revenue ~~for 2024 contracted to roughly $5 million~~ ==in 2024 resumed at $4.418 million before stepping up sharply to $70.918 million in 2025==, even as AST's first five operational BlueBird Block 1 satellites reached orbit.

~~The decline was not a setback in any operational sense. It reflected the natural exhaustion of early-stage engineering services contracts with MNO partners~~ ==The lumpy trajectory reflected the timing of engineering services contracts with MNO partners== — arrangements under which carriers such as Vodafone and Rakuten had contributed to the design and validation work surrounding the BlueWalker 3 prototype launched in September 2022 and the subsequent BlueBird platform architecture. ~~As those bilateral development agreements concluded, the revenue they had generated rolled off without being replaced by commercial service billings, which remained immaterial as of the frozen snapshot date.~~ ==As those bilateral development agreements concluded the revenue they had generated rolled off in 2023, then resumed in 2024 and accelerated sharply in 2025 as product revenue from gateway equipment and early service revenue began to flow, even though continuous SpaceMobile commercial service to MNO end-customers remained pending as of the frozen snapshot date.== The trajectory was a compressed illustration of the pre-revenue phase: a company spending at scale to build the infrastructure that would eventually invert the income statement entirely.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD m) | Nature of Revenue |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | ~$11 | Engineering services, partner contributions |
| 2023 | ~~$12~~ ==0== | ~~Engineering services, partner contributions~~ ==No GAAP revenue== |
| 2024 | ~~$5~~ ==$4.418== | ~~Residual engineering services; commercial service immaterial~~ ==Engineering services plus early gateway equipment and service billings== |
| ==2025== | ==$70.918== | ==Step-up driven by gateway product revenue and service revenue ahead of continuous commercial launch== |

## The SPAC and the initial capital stack

AST SpaceMobile reached the public markets on 7 April 2021 through a merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp, a blank-check vehicle that had been assembled specifically to take the Midland, Texas company public. The transaction was structured as a conventional SPAC business combination with a concurrent PIPE placement, and it delivered the proceeds AST needed to move BlueWalker 3 from design to fabrication. The listing placed the company on NASDAQ under the ticker ASTS, and gave it a public currency — critical for subsequent capital formation in an industry where the capital requirements are front-loaded and the revenue curves are long.

The SPAC structure also locked in the first tier of strategic equity. Vodafone and Rakuten Mobile, both of which had signed commercial framework agreements with AST before the listing, retained meaningful stakes through the transaction. Their presence on the cap table served a dual signalling function: it anchored the commercial thesis for public market investors, and it gave AST a cost-of-capital advantage in subsequent raises by demonstrating that sophisticated telecommunications operators were willing to put equity at risk behind the technology.

## Strategic equity: carriers as co-investors

Perhaps the most distinctive feature of AST SpaceMobile's capital structure relative to other satellite-sector SPAC graduates of the same vintage — Momentus, BlackSky, Spire — was the depth of its MNO equity syndicate. By the time BlueBird Block 1 launched in September 2024, AST had assembled a roster of strategic investors that included Vodafone, Rakuten Mobile, AT&T, and Google, each of which had converted commercial alignment into ownership stakes. ==AT&T and Google joined the cap table through the January 2024 strategic investment round, not the 2021 SPAC/PIPE.==

AT&T's investment was particularly significant in strategic terms. ~~The carrier signed a multi-year commercial agreement with AST that positioned it as the anchor US distribution partner, and then followed that agreement with a meaningful direct equity commitment.~~ ==The carrier made a direct equity commitment as part of AST's January 2024 strategic investment round, and on 15 May 2024 signed a definitive multi-year commercial agreement that positioned it as the anchor US distribution partner.== Google's participation, disclosed in the context of AST's 2024 capital raise, added a further dimension: the search company's interest in direct-to-cell connectivity aligned with its broader mobile ecosystem strategy and provided AST with incremental technical credibility.

> "We believe we are building the first and only space-based cellular broadband network that will be accessible by the over 5 billion people with standard mobile devices," Abel Avellan said, characterising the commercial logic that had drawn MNO equity into the capital structure.

Rakuten Mobile's position reflected a different strategic rationale. The Japanese carrier, which operates a cloud-native terrestrial network under Tarō Kono's reform-era mobile liberalisation, had identified AST's coverage extension capability as a way to address Japan's substantial unserved rural geography without the capital intensity of additional ground infrastructure. Its equity position thus functioned simultaneously as a hedge against coverage cost and a strategic option on the satellite layer of a future converged network.

## Subsequent capital raises: feeding the constellation machine

The SPAC proceeds were never intended to fund full-constellation deployment. The architecture of AST's financing strategy depended on milestone-gated capital formation: demonstrate the technology, sign the MNO agreements, build investor conviction, then raise larger tranches at progressively more advantageous terms as the risk profile compressed. That logic held, if imperfectly.

The company executed multiple equity offerings between 2021 and 2024, taking advantage of periods of elevated share price — particularly following positive BlueWalker 3 test results in late 2022 and early 2023, when the satellite established direct voice calls to unmodified smartphones and set records for data throughput in the direct-to-cell segment. Each successful demonstration gave AST a window to raise at terms that diluted existing holders less than the capital would otherwise have cost.

Convertible debt instruments supplemented the equity raises, providing a mechanism to access capital without immediate dilution while retaining the conversion optionality that investors in high-growth, pre-revenue technology companies typically demand. The convertible notes issued as part of AST's 2024 financing round — a raise that brought in several hundred million dollars ahead of the Block 1 launches — were structured to give the company runway through the deployment phase and into the early commercial period.

The combined effect of these instruments was a capital structure that, by mid-2024, was substantially more complex than the clean equity-only balance sheet the SPAC had produced three years earlier. Warrants, convertible instruments, and multiple tranches of common stock issued at varying prices created a layered equity overhang that market participants tracked carefully as a potential headwind against share price appreciation in the commercial phase.

## Operating economics and the cost of pre-commercial scale

AST's operating losses over the 2022–2024 period were substantial and structurally predictable. The company was simultaneously carrying the capital expenditure of satellite manufacturing — a programme with no comparable cost-reduction roadmap to SpaceX's Falcon 9 amortisation, though it benefited from using SpaceX as its launch provider — and the operating expenditure of a growing engineering organisation in Midland, Texas, where it had expanded its antenna fabrication and testing capabilities, and in Midland and internationally where it maintained its software and network engineering teams.

Research and development expenditure dominated the income statement below the revenue line. The development of BlueWalker 3, its integration and testing campaign, the subsequent redesign work that produced the BlueBird platform architecture, and the further scaling effort to generate the Block 2 design — which AST described as carrying approximately two to three times the antenna aperture of Block 1 — each required sustained engineering headcount and equipment expenditure that ran well ahead of any offsetting revenue.

Stock-based compensation, a standard feature of the pre-revenue technology company income statement, added a non-cash layer to reported losses that inflated the headline figure without affecting the cash burn that mattered most to the runway calculation. On a cash basis, AST was burning at a rate that made its capital raise cadence structurally necessary rather than opportunistic.

## Cash position and constellation deployment economics

The economics of deploying a low earth orbit satellite constellation at commercial scale are not linear. The per-satellite manufacturing cost carries significant fixed overhead in the early production batches, where tooling, test infrastructure, and engineering iteration dominate unit economics. As production volumes increase, the learning curve and supply chain maturation compress per-unit costs — a dynamic that AST was actively pursuing as it moved toward Block 2.

Launch costs, with SpaceX Falcon 9 as the primary launch provider under the Transporter and dedicated rideshare programmes, were a known and relatively stable variable. The first five BlueBird Block 1 satellites reached orbit on 12 September 2024 aboard a Falcon 9, a launch that demonstrated both the practical execution capability of AST's operations team and the depth of its relationship with SpaceX~~, which had itself been a shareholder in AST at earlier stages of the company's development~~.

Block 2's larger physical footprint — the expanded phased-array antenna being the primary driver — implied higher per-satellite manufacturing cost relative to Block 1. AST management had consistently framed the Block 2 investment as justified by the substantially higher capacity per satellite, which in turn would lower the cost per gigabyte delivered to partner networks and improve the unit economics of the commercial service model. The argument was structurally sound but contingent on achieving the production volume necessary for the learning curve to flatten.

Through the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, AST's cash position reflected the proceeds of its 2024 capital raise, partially offset by the continuing operating burn and the capital expenditure associated with the Block 2 development and deployment programme. The company had stated a capital requirement extending through the ramp to commercial scale that implied further capital formation would likely be necessary unless the commercial service revenue conversion from its MNO partners — particularly AT&T and Verizon in the United States and Vodafone across its international footprint — accelerated materially.

| Capital Event | Approximate Timing | Strategic Significance |
|---|---|---|
| SPAC merger + PIPE (New Providence) | April 2021 | Initial public market capital; Vodafone/Rakuten equity locked in |
| Post-SPAC equity raises (multiple tranches) | 2021–2023 | Milestone-gated dilution; timed to positive technical results |
| AT&T + Google strategic investment + convertible debt | ~~2024~~ ==January 2024== | Anchor US carrier equity; pre-Block 1 launch runway extension |
| Block 1 launches | September 2024 | Operational proof of concept; precondition for commercial billings |

The financing architecture AST assembled between its 2017 founding and the deployment of its first operational satellites was unusual in the satellite sector for the degree to which it aligned commercial partners' economic interests with the company's own survival. The MNO equity holders had both a financial incentive and a commercial rationale to support AST's capital raises and, eventually, to convert their framework agreements into revenue-generating service deployments. Whether that alignment would prove sufficient to fund the Block 2 deployment at the scale and pace required to establish commercial viability before the capital structure required further dilutive action remained the central financial question as of the frozen snapshot date.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The standard toolkit of equity valuation — trailing earnings multiples, EV/EBITDA, dividend yield — applies awkwardly, and in some cases not at all, to AST SpaceMobile as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026. The company's revenue base as last reported remained dominated by engineering services and pre-commercial partner contributions; ~~the $5 million of 2024 revenue reflected a step-down from the 2022–2023 run rate as engineering-service contributions from strategic MNO partners wound down ahead of commercial service launches~~ ==the $4.4 million of 2024 GAAP revenue arrived after a year of zero reported revenue in 2023, with 2025 revenue then stepping sharply higher to $70.9 million as initial gateway-equipment product revenue and service revenue began to flow alongside engineering-service contributions from strategic MNO partners==. Meaningful commercial mobile revenue — the recurring MNO revenue-share flows from AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, and the broader fifty-plus-operator partnership portfolio — had not yet reached a scale that would anchor a conventional multiple. What the market was pricing, therefore, was not a stream of earnings but a probability-weighted option on a new telecommunications infrastructure category.

## The Numerics of an Option-Value Stock

Reasoning from AST SpaceMobile's most recently filed share count and the trading range visible in the weeks approaching the snapshot date, the company's diluted share count — inclusive of issued Class A and Class B common stock, vested restricted units, and shares underlying outstanding convertible instruments — is estimated in the range of 340–390 million. At a stock trading range of approximately ~~$18–$26~~ ==$63.87–$105.86== per share through May 2026, the implied market capitalisation sits in a band of roughly ~~$6.1 billion to $10.1 billion~~ ==$22 billion to $41 billion==; call the midpoint approximately ~~$7.5 billion~~ ==$32 billion==. Adding the company's net debt position — convertible notes and other facilities accumulated through successive capital raises to fund constellation deployment — elevates the enterprise value to an estimated ~~$8.5–$9.5 billion~~ ==$23–$43 billion==. These figures are reasoned from available share-count disclosures and recent price ranges, not from a live data pull, and carry commensurate uncertainty.

Against trailing twelve-month revenue ~~that, extrapolating from the 2024 figure, may reside in the low tens of millions~~ ==of roughly $70 million on the basis of 2025 GAAP results, supplemented by initial Q1 2026 product and service flows==, EV/Sales on a trailing basis is not a useful anchor. The figure analysts and growth-oriented investors actually trade against is forward EV/Revenue, using consensus estimates for the twelve to eighteen months ahead. ~~If street-consensus 2026 revenue estimates cluster around $200–$350 million — reflecting initial commercial launches with AT&T and Verizon in the United States plus early international MNO flows — the NTM EV/Sales multiple sits somewhere between 27x and 48x.~~ ==Taking management's full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $150–$200 million as the anchor — reflecting initial commercial launches with AT&T and Verizon in the United States plus early international MNO flows — the NTM EV/Sales multiple sits somewhere between roughly 115x and 285x.== These are not multiples ~~traditional telecom or satellite infrastructure buyers would tolerate; they are growth-technology multiples applied to an infrastructure business~~ ==traditional telecom, satellite infrastructure, or even most growth-technology peers would tolerate==, and they price in a steep revenue trajectory.

## A Stock That Has Already Been Re-Rated Twice

The history of ASTS since its [April 7, 2021 SPAC listing](https://investors.ast-science.com) with New Providence Acquisition Corp is itself an argument about how the market processes binary technological uncertainty. At listing, the stock priced near $10, implying roughly $2–3 billion of market capitalisation calibrated to early-stage constellation milestones. Through 2022 and into 2023, as cash burn continued, technology risk remained unvalidated, and Starlink Direct to Cell emerged as a credible competitive threat, the stock de-rated sharply — reaching a trough in the $3–6 range and implying enterprise values well below $2 billion. In that phase, the market discounted the probability of execution failure, capital exhaustion, and competitive displacement in roughly equal measure.

The September 2022 BlueWalker 3 prototype launch provided partial reassurance on technology risk, but it was the [September 12, 2024 launch of the first five BlueBird Block 1 operational satellites](https://investors.ast-science.com) aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rideshare — and subsequent confirmations of commercial-grade direct-to-cell voice and data throughput from unmodified handsets — that triggered a full re-rating. ~~The stock moved from the mid-single digits to the mid-to-high teens and beyond in the months following.~~ ==The stock moved from the mid-single digits through the teens and ultimately into the $60–$100+ band visible in May 2026.== Strategic commercial commitments from AT&T and Verizon compressed perceived execution risk and expanded the multiple investors were willing to apply to the forward revenue story. By the frozen snapshot, ASTS had traversed from deep-discount venture proxy to growth-technology infrastructure — a journey of many turns of EV/NTM Revenue expansion from trough to current.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

No listed peer replicates the AST SpaceMobile model precisely — a MNO-partnership direct-to-cell constellation selling recurring service access to mobile operators rather than to end-consumers. The closest comparables are legacy satellite mobile operators and newer direct-to-device ventures, all of which trade at materially lower multiples, reflecting their more established but lower-growth profiles.

| Company | Ticker | Model | EV/NTM Revenue | EV/NTM EBITDA | Revenue Growth (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AST SpaceMobile | ASTS | Direct-to-cell LEO, MNO rev-share | ~~27–48x~~ ==~115–285x== | NM | High (commercial ramp onset) |
| Iridium Communications | IRDM | Voice/IoT LEO, direct subscriber | ~5x | ~12x | Low-mid single digit |
| Globalstar | GSAT | Direct-to-device spectrum (Apple) | ~7–9x | ~20x | Moderate (Apple service fees) |
| Viasat | VSAT | GEO/MEO broadband, in-flight | ~1.5–2x | ~7–9x | Low single digit |
| Planet Labs | PL | Earth-observation LEO, data services | ~5–7x | NM | Mid-teen |
| EchoStar | SATS | GEO broadband, spectrum assets | ~1–2x | ~6–8x | Flat to negative |

*Multiples estimated from available analyst consensus and market data as of the frozen snapshot; precise figures subject to real-time market movements.*

The premium ASTS commands over every listed peer reflects the optionality embedded in the MNO partnership structure and the sheer scale of the addressable subscriber base — potentially billions of existing mobile subscribers who could access space-based connectivity without a device upgrade. Iridium and Globalstar, the natural model comparators, are mature businesses with predictable but modest growth profiles. The ASTS multiple premium is, in essence, the market's bet that the revenue ramp will be steep enough to justify an entry price that looks egregious on any backward-looking basis.

## What the Current Price Implies: A Reverse-Engineered DCF

Reverse-engineering the current enterprise value of roughly ~~$9 billion~~ ==$33 billion== into a cash-flow trajectory provides a useful sanity check on embedded assumptions. Assuming the company eventually reaches a steady-state EBITDA margin in the 40–55% range — plausible for a largely fixed-cost satellite infrastructure layer delivering software-economics service revenue — and trades at 15–18x mature EBITDA upon reaching scale, the current EV requires approximately ~~$500–$600 million~~ ==$1.8–$2.2 billion== of steady-state EBITDA to represent fair value at a 10–12% discount rate with a seven-to-ten year horizon.

At a 45% EBITDA margin, that implies roughly ~~$1.1–$1.3 billion~~ ==$4.0–$4.9 billion== of mature annual revenue. For a company targeting a subscriber base running into hundreds of millions globally, ~~$1.2 billion~~ ==$4.5 billion== of annual revenue represents approximately ~~2–3% penetration of a five-billion-subscriber global mobile market at a $2–3 per subscriber per year effective revenue-share rate. That penetration level is not heroic.~~ ==6–10% penetration of a five-billion-subscriber global mobile market at a $9–$15 per subscriber per year effective revenue-share rate. That penetration level is demanding but defensible over a multi-decade infrastructure rollout.== The long-run mathematics of the addressable market make the bull case structurally easier to defend than the near-term execution path, which is precisely the nature of the valuation risk.

## Three Scenarios

**Bull case — $45–$60 per share.** Block 2 deployment executes on schedule through 2025–2026, adding significant capacity per satellite given the ~2–3x antenna-area advantage over Block 1. AT&T and Verizon commercial launches reach millions of US subscribers by end of 2026; international MNO partners including Vodafone, Rakuten Mobile, MTN Africa, Bell Canada, and Telstra convert pre-commercial agreements to revenue-generating service at pace. 2027 revenue reaches $700 million–$1 billion. Analysts begin applying a 15–20x forward EV/Revenue multiple to a growth franchise now demonstrably executing at scale. At $900 million of 2027 revenue, 18x forward EV/Sales, and a diluted share count of approximately 380 million, the implied price lands in the $40–$55 range. The bull case requires Block 2 to prove out technically and MNO subscriber adoption to ramp materially faster than the historical satellite-service adoption curve would suggest.

**Base case — $20–$30 per share.** Block 2 launches proceed with modest delays of one to two quarters; initial commercial MNO deployments in the US generate meaningful but not transformative subscriber counts in the low-to-mid millions. 2027 revenue reaches $300–$500 million. The market applies 15–20x forward EV/Sales to a more measured growth trajectory. At $400 million of 2027 revenue, 17x NTM EV/Sales, and the current share-count range, the implied value sits in the $22–$28 range~~ — roughly in line with the midpoint of recent trading~~ ==, materially below the May 2026 trading range and embedding a substantial multiple compression as the growth-vs-execution debate narrows toward execution==. The base case assumes steady but unspectacular commercial conversion and continued but manageable dilution from capital raises to fund ongoing Block 2 deployment.

**Bear case — $7–$12 per share.** Block 2 faces material technical or launch-cadence delays. Starlink Direct to Cell — operating under SpaceX's structural cost advantage and leveraging Starlink's existing carrier relationships — captures the first-mover advantage in large North American and European markets before ASTS reaches competitive coverage density. MNO commercial-conversion timelines slip to 2028 and beyond, undermining the revenue ramp that justifies the current multiple. Capital raises accelerate dilution beyond 450 million shares. The market re-applies a venture-stage discount to what looks again like an infrastructure buildout with uncertain competitive standing. At 10x NTM EV/Sales on $150 million of 2027 revenue and approximately 450 million diluted shares, the implied price falls to approximately $8–$12.

## The Consensus Gap

The principal divergence between street consensus and the dossier's read is competitive intensity. Models that have driven the post-Block 1 re-rating appear to price the MNO partnership structure as essentially defensible — that carriers globally will prefer a purpose-built MNO-aligned constellation over Starlink's direct-to-consumer heritage. That judgment may prove correct if the thesis holds that MNOs will resist becoming dumb pipes beneath a vertically integrated SpaceX offering that competes directly with their own subscriber relationships. But the asymmetric downside risk is that Starlink Direct to Cell's price-to-performance trajectory, backstopped by SpaceX's unmatched launch economics, compresses MNO willingness to pay before ASTS accumulates the satellite count needed to offer competitive coverage density across its key markets. The current multiple embeds a meaningful probability weight on the MNO-alliance outcome; a cautious position weights the Starlink competitive displacement scenario more heavily than the consensus currently implies.

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarters through BlueWalker, BlueBird, and MNO partnership milestones
chapters.body:
## The SPAC Debut and the Weight of the Promise

When AST SpaceMobile completed its business combination with New Providence Acquisition Corp in April 2021, the listing represented more than a conventional path to public capital. It was the moment Abel Avellan's founding thesis — that a low Earth orbit constellation could provide cellular broadband directly to standard, unmodified handsets — came under the scrutiny of quarterly earnings cycles. The company arrived on NASDAQ under the ticker ASTS with gross proceeds from the merger and concurrent PIPE positioned to fund the constellation's first operational phase. The early post-SPAC quarters established the revenue baseline that would define the pre-commercial period: engineering services and partner-contribution revenues of roughly $11 million in 2022 and ~~$12 million in 2023~~ ==zero GAAP revenue in 2023==, against substantial operating losses reflecting the capital-intensive build-out of what Avellan described as the world's only space-based cellular broadband network designed to interoperate with standard mobile devices without hardware modification.

The investor communications from the first post-SPAC quarters carried the structural tension inherent to any pre-commercial infrastructure company in a growth phase. Avellan and CFO Andrew Johnson articulated the strategic case in terms of total addressable market — roughly five billion people with limited or no mobile broadband connectivity — against a timeline requiring both technical execution of a novel satellite design and commercial alignment with global mobile network operators. The financial profile provided little to evaluate beyond the scale of operating losses; the investment case rested on the technology's credibility, which only a flight demonstration could establish.

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Physics

The single most consequential event in the post-SPAC period was the launch of the BlueWalker 3 test satellite aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 on September 10, 2022. BlueWalker 3 was not a commercial satellite but a full-scale prototype — a platform designed to validate the core technical claims underpinning the entire business model. The satellite carried an approximately 693-square-foot (64 square metre) phased-array antenna that, upon deployment in late October 2022, constituted the largest commercial communications array placed in low Earth orbit to that date. The engineering challenge was exacting: to serve standard unmodified handsets, the satellite needed to replicate, from roughly 500 kilometres altitude, the signal characteristics that a terrestrial cell tower provides metres from the user.

> "BlueWalker 3 is the foundation of our plan to provide affordable broadband to unserved and underserved communities using standard smartphones — with no new hardware required," Avellan said around the time of the launch, as reported in company communications.

The months following antenna deployment delivered on the core technical promise. In April 2023, the company announced completion of what it described as the first space-based cellular broadband calls made on standard mobile handsets, conducted across AT&T's network in the United States and Rakuten's network in Japan. The demonstrations used unmodified 4G LTE devices — the operational proof that the physics worked as designed. On Q1 and Q2 2023 earnings calls, Avellan was able to shift the investor narrative from technical speculation to demonstrated capability, even as the financial profile remained squarely pre-commercial.

> "We have now proven that our satellites can talk directly to standard, unmodified mobile phones," Avellan told investors following the broadband demonstrations. "This is the capability that the world's mobile operators have been waiting for."

## The Partnership Architecture Solidifies

The period between the BlueWalker 3 demonstrations and the BlueBird Block 1 launch was defined less by revenue than by the expansion of the mobile network operator partnership framework. The strategic logic was structural: AST SpaceMobile did not intend to serve end users directly. The SpaceMobile network would operate as a supplemental layer on top of existing MNO networks, with MNO partners providing spectrum and customer relationships while AST provided the space segment.

By late 2023, the company had assembled a roster of MNO partnerships covering a substantial portion of the world's mobile subscriber base.

| MNO Partner | Geography | Strategic Equity Participation |
|---|---|---|
| AT&T | United States | ~~Yes~~ ==Yes (added January 2024)== |
| ~~Verizon~~ ==Verizon (definitive commercial agreement announced October 8, 2025)== | United States | ~~Board designation~~ ==—== |
| Vodafone | Europe (multi-market) | Yes |
| Rakuten Mobile | Japan | Yes |
| Bell Canada | Canada | — |
| Telefonica | Latin America / Europe | — |
| Orange | France / multi-market | — |

The equity participation from ~~Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, and Google — announced across the 2021–2023 period~~ ==Vodafone and Rakuten across the 2021–2023 period, joined by AT&T and Google through the January 2024 strategic investment== — simultaneously validated the technical and commercial thesis while providing capital supplementing the post-SPAC proceeds and subsequent equity and convertible debt issuances. Each equity partnership carried an additional structural dimension: the MNO partners were providing the licensed cellular spectrum the satellites would use to deliver service to their own subscribers, aligning the commercial interests of both parties in a way that made each equity announcement a proxy confirmation of technical credibility as much as a capital event. The board composition reflected the architecture directly, with ~~representatives from AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, and Rakuten~~ ==nominees designated by AT&T, Vodafone, and American Tower== holding or designating seats alongside Avellan's consolidated Chairman-CEO-President role.

The company's balance sheet management through this period reflected the fundamental challenge of funding a capital-intensive constellation on engineering-services revenue. Multiple capital raises maintained the runway required to reach the BlueBird production milestone, while the MNO partner contributions provided steady if modest revenue — $11 million in 2022, ~~$12 million in 2023~~ ==zero GAAP revenue in 2023== — that ~~validated the commercial relationships without yet monetising them at scale~~ ==left the commercial relationships unmonetised at the GAAP line==.

## BlueBird Block 1: Transition to Operations

On September 12, 2024, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off carrying the first five BlueBird Block 1 operational satellites — the transition from prototype validation to initial operational capability. The Block 1 design drew directly on BlueWalker 3 learnings but was engineered as a production satellite rather than a technology demonstrator. The five-satellite manifest was the opening tranche of a constellation that, in management's articulated planning, would require substantially more capacity to deliver the coverage and throughput necessary for broad commercial service.

> "Today we begin the transition from technology demonstration to commercial operations," Avellan said following the September 2024 launch. "Our mobile operator partners around the world have been waiting for this moment. We are now building the constellation."

The BlueBird Block 1 launch also coincided with a revealing inflection in the revenue line. The ~~$5 million~~ ==$4.4 million== in reported 2024 revenues — ~~lower in absolute terms than the 2022 and 2023 engineering-services baselines~~ ==lower than the roughly $11 million 2022 engineering-services baseline but above the zero GAAP revenue posted in 2023== — reflected the structural transition away from the pre-commercial partnership contribution model. Engineering services agreements with MNO partners that had generated pre-commercial revenue wound down as those partners prepared to convert to commercial service arrangements; the commercial service revenues that would replace them had not yet reached material scale. The operating loss profile remained substantial, reflecting ongoing constellation deployment costs, but the character of the business had changed from perpetual pre-commercial to early operational.

## Toward Commercial Scale: Q4 2024 Through Q1 2026

The quarters following the BlueBird Block 1 launch ~~established the commercial conversion cadence that strategic investors had spent three years anticipating. AT&T and select MNO partners began offering service to subscribers in late 2024 as limited-availability programmes, expanding operationally as the space segment was matured. The scale remained modest relative to the addressable market, but the service relationship with a paying MNO partner — rather than an engineering-contribution relationship — marked a structural threshold the quarterly earnings calls had been targeting since 2021.~~ ==advanced the commercial agreement architecture rather than the commercial service line itself. AT&T's definitive commercial agreement was announced May 15, 2024, and Verizon's followed on October 8, 2025. Through the Q1 2026 10-Q, however, the company still described SpaceMobile Service initiation as pending limited, noncontinuous activation, meaning the structural threshold of a paying MNO service relationship at scale that the quarterly earnings calls had been targeting since 2021 remained ahead rather than behind the snapshot date.==

The Block 2 satellite design entered the development and production pipeline in parallel with the Block 1 operational ramp. With antenna area roughly two to three times greater per satellite than Block 1, the Block 2 design represented the primary capacity vehicle for commercial scale: more aperture per satellite translated directly into higher throughput per orbit pass and greater concurrent subscriber capacity. Management positioned Block 2 deployment, extending into 2025 and 2026, as the scaling mechanism that would convert the initial operational capability into a commercially material constellation.

Avellan's investor communications through Q4 2024 and across 2025 returned repeatedly to the structural commercial proposition: direct-to-cell operated in the cellular bands licensed to MNO partners rather than requiring dedicated spectrum allocations or specialist handset hardware, offering a unit economics argument that conventional satellite broadband models could not replicate for the mass-market mobile use case.

Through Q1 2026, the financial profile continued to reflect an early-stage commercial operation: revenues remained substantially below the level required to offset constellation deployment costs, and the company's strategic execution remained contingent on continued capital market access and commercial conversion of the MNO partnership portfolio into paying service revenues at scale. The trajectory, nonetheless, had shifted irrevocably from the speculative to the operational — from the physics demonstration of BlueWalker 3 through the first five BlueBird satellites to a growing roster of MNO partners preparing to offer space-based coverage to subscribers who had never known reliable mobile service.
