chapters.title: AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, broader MNO portfolio, and the satellite supply chain
chapters.body:
## The operator alliance: building the wholesale satellite layer

The commercial logic underpinning AST SpaceMobile's business model rested on a counterintuitive proposition: that the world's largest mobile network operators would willingly pay a startup to extend their networks into space. By the time the first five BlueBird Block 1 satellites reached orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 on September 12, 2024, AST had spent seven years assembling the partnerships to make that proposition credible.

The architecture is wholesale, not retail. AST does not sell directly to consumers, does not build handsets, and does not operate billing infrastructure. Instead, it sells satellite connectivity as a layer that mobile operators embed into their existing networks — subscribers connect to BlueBird satellites using the same smartphones and the same SIM cards they already carry, billed through their existing carrier accounts. The MNO assumes the customer relationship; AST provides the coverage infrastructure. This model required that AST secure MNO partners before it could demonstrate commercial service, making the partnership portfolio the commercial asset in the same way that tower companies treat their tenancy agreements.

## AT&T and Verizon: spectrum anchor and US commercial cornerstone

The two US carrier giants occupied a structural position in AST's framework that went beyond revenue. AT&T and Verizon were not merely distribution partners; they were the spectrum contributors whose terrestrial frequency licenses enabled AST's satellites to legally operate over American territory.

AST SpaceMobile's satellites did not use dedicated satellite spectrum allocations. Instead, they operated in the same LTE frequency bands — including AWS, PCS, and 700 MHz bands — that AT&T and Verizon held through their terrestrial licenses. The technical and regulatory insight behind the company's founding was that a satellite carrying a sufficiently large phased-array antenna could concentrate radio energy precisely enough to illuminate a standard handset using these existing bands without causing unacceptable interference to the terrestrial networks beneath. The spectrum coordination between satellite and ground was managed jointly between AST and the carrier partners.

For BlueWalker 3 testing from late 2022 through 2023, the Federal Communications Commission issued Special Temporary Authorities granting AST permission to use licensed terrestrial bands from orbit. AT&T participated in the first direct-to-smartphone voice call demonstration using BlueWalker 3 — the satellite transmitted and received LTE signals to and from an unmodified Samsung Galaxy S22 on an AT&T connection from approximately 700 kilometres above the earth's surface. Verizon subsequently conducted equivalent demonstrations. ~~Both carriers signed multi-year commercial service agreements and made direct equity investments in AST prior to the SPAC listing — pre-commercial validation of the business model that was visible on the company's cap table before any material revenue had materialized.~~ ==AT&T's strategic investment in AST was announced in January 2024, alongside Google, with AT&T's definitive commercial service agreement following on May 15, 2024; Verizon's definitive commercial agreement was announced on October 8, 2025, after the September 2024 Block 1 launch. AT&T's equity position became visible on the company's cap table well before material revenue had materialized, while Verizon's relationship with AST developed primarily through commercial rather than equity channels.==

The practical significance of ~~those equity positions~~ ==AT&T's equity position== extended beyond the check ~~amounts~~ ==amount==. ~~AT&T and Verizon's stakes as shareholders aligned their~~ ==AT&T's stake as a shareholder, combined with Verizon's deepening commercial commitments, aligned both carriers'== regulatory and lobbying interests with AST's own at a moment when the FCC framework governing satellite direct-to-device was still being written. Both carriers had an incentive to support favorable spectrum-coordination rules because doing so protected the value of ~~their own equity positions~~ ==their respective commercial commitments and, in AT&T's case, its equity stake==.

## Vodafone and Rakuten: strategic anchors in international markets

Vodafone Group represented AST's most consequential international partnership. The British-headquartered carrier, which by the mid-2020s operated or held stakes in networks across Europe, Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Asia, offered AST two things simultaneously: equity capital and spectrum footprint. As both equity holder and commercial partner, Vodafone provided international spectrum rights across dozens of regulatory jurisdictions, removing one of the principal barriers to non-US commercial service. A mobile operator's terrestrial spectrum licenses are national assets, and AST's constellation required local spectrum rights in each country where it intended to operate.

Vodafone's commercial partnership encompassed the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Spain, and large portions of the company's sub-Saharan African footprint — markets with substantial rural and maritime coverage gaps that BlueBird's satellite layer could address. The carrier's early involvement predated the SPAC listing, making Vodafone one of the handful of institutional validators that accepted technical and regulatory risk before a single operational satellite was in orbit.

Rakuten Mobile's partnership occupied a different strategic position. The Japanese carrier, which launched Japan's first cloud-native, fully virtualised mobile network in 2020, brought engineering credibility and a specific market advantage: Japan's regulatory environment for satellite services had historically been cautious, and Rakuten's domestic sponsorship smoothed the approval pathway. Rakuten's investment in AST reflected a broader thesis about low-Earth-orbit connectivity filling the rural and suburban coverage gaps that Rakuten's still-maturing 4G network had not fully closed. Like Vodafone, Rakuten held equity and contributed access to Japan's frequency bands — making its partnership simultaneously financial and operational.

## The broader MNO portfolio: 50 countries and counting

Beyond the headline names, AST had by the time of the 2024 BlueBird launch assembled commercial agreements spanning more than fifty countries. Bell Canada extended the coverage logic northward into Canada's vast Arctic and rural territories, where terrestrial cellular economics had never supported build-out. Telstra, Australia's incumbent carrier, offered analogous access to Australia's enormous landmass, where direct-to-cell coverage could serve communities separated by hundreds of kilometres from the nearest cell tower.

MTN Group, the Johannesburg-headquartered pan-African carrier with operations across more than twenty African markets, represented arguably the single largest addressable population among AST's MNO partners. Sub-Saharan Africa's mobile penetration rate — already among the fastest growing in the world — masked a structural coverage problem: the continent's population density patterns made terrestrial infrastructure economics unworkable across large rural and peri-urban areas. MTN's partnership with AST was an acknowledgment that satellite-layer wholesale coverage could close gaps that MTN's own capital expenditure programme could not economically address.

The cumulative geographic reach of the MNO portfolio meant that once AST's constellation achieved sufficient density, commercially addressable subscribers would number in the billions — a figure Avellan returned to repeatedly in investor communications as the foundational argument for the company's long-run revenue potential.

## Satellite manufacturing: phased-array engineering at scale in Midland

The physical expression of AST SpaceMobile's technological ambition was the BlueBird satellite, built principally at the company's Midland, Texas facility. The defining engineering challenge was the phased-array antenna: to illuminate a standard smartphone from low Earth orbit, the satellite must concentrate radio energy with extraordinary precision, which in practice required an antenna aperture measured in tens of square metres.

BlueWalker 3, launched in September 2022 as the technology demonstration satellite, carried an unfurled phased-array approximately 64 square metres in area — the largest commercial communications array in low Earth orbit at the time of its deployment. The BlueBird Block 1 satellites carried antennas of comparable aperture. Block 2, under development through 2025 and 2026, was designed at approximately two to three times the antenna area, targeting commensurately higher per-satellite capacity — a scaling approach intended to reduce the cost per delivered gigabyte with each successive generation.

Manufacturing the phased-array antenna required integrating thousands of individual radiating elements into a structure capable of surviving launch loads, deploying reliably in the thermal extremes of low Earth orbit, and maintaining phase coherence across the full aperture throughout operations. AST developed the phased-array design internally, treating it as a core proprietary asset, while sourcing other bus components — solar arrays, reaction wheels, propulsion systems, star trackers — from specialist suppliers. The Midland facility combined satellite assembly with antenna fabrication, a degree of vertical integration reflecting both the novelty of the antenna technology and the absence of any off-the-shelf supplier capable of delivering phased arrays at the required scale.

## Launch services: SpaceX as infrastructure partner

For the September 2024 Block 1 deployment, AST turned to SpaceX's Falcon 9, the vehicle that had by that point become the workhorse of the commercial satellite industry. The five Block 1 satellites launched as a batch on September 12, 2024, from Cape Canaveral into low Earth orbit at approximately 500 kilometres altitude. The Falcon 9's reliability record, its cost per kilogram to low Earth orbit, and SpaceX's experience coordinating large constellation deployments made it the natural choice for a programme whose per-satellite mass was substantial relative to the smallsat rideshare alternatives.

The relationship with SpaceX carried competitive complexity that investors did not overlook. SpaceX's own Starlink Direct to Cell programme — a direct-to-device service built on the Starlink constellation in commercial partnership with T-Mobile — competed in the same market segment as AST and used the same Falcon 9 for its own launches. AST was simultaneously dependent on a competitor's launch infrastructure and contesting that competitor's satellite service offering. Avellan addressed the distinction in investor forums by emphasising that AST's MNO-neutral wholesale model — serving AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and dozens of other carriers rather than a single operator — created a broader commercial addressable market than any service tied to one carrier's subscriber base.

## Regulatory architecture: FCC, ITU, and the spectrum coordination framework

The regulatory foundation supporting AST's commercial deployment rested on two interlocking structures. Domestically, the FCC's willingness to authorise terrestrial spectrum use from orbit — first through Special Temporary Authorities for BlueWalker 3 and subsequently through broader licensing under Part 25 satellite frameworks combined with the terrestrial mobile rules — created the legal basis for US commercial service. The coordination mechanism between AST's satellite beams and the terrestrial networks of AT&T and Verizon formed a novel regulatory category that the FCC's Space Bureau worked through incrementally alongside the company and its carrier partners over the course of several years.

Internationally, the International Telecommunication Union's coordination procedures governed AST's ability to operate in partner-country frequency bands without causing harmful interference to other licensed systems. Each MNO partnership carried implicit spectrum rights — the carrier's domestic licenses extended, through the AST commercial agreement and applicable national regulation, to cover satellite-layer transmissions in that carrier's frequency bands. The ITU filing position for AST's satellite network, maintained through the coordination process, underpinned the legal certainty that investors and commercial partners required before committing capital to a deployment programme eventually measured in hundreds of satellites.

chapters.title: Where AST sits against Starlink Direct to Cell, Lynk Global, and broader satellite competitors
chapters.body:
## A Market That Looked Uncontested, Then Didn't

When Abel Avellan assembled the first engineering team in Midland, Texas in 2017, direct-to-cell satellite connectivity for unmodified smartphones was a concept that the industry's incumbents had largely dismissed as physically impossible. The link budget arithmetic seemed unforgiving: a handheld device radiating a fraction of a watt against the vacuum of low-Earth orbit, with no dish, no special firmware, no cooperative ground infrastructure. By the time BlueWalker 3 demonstrated two-way voice and data in late 2022, the premise had shifted from improbable to proven — and the competitive map shifted with it.

The company that had spent five years building toward a largely uncontested market found itself, by 2024, in a three-front competitive environment: SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell program scaling aggressively; Lynk Global pursuing a narrowband niche from a well-funded private position; and Apple's emergency satellite feature quietly redefining consumer expectations without ever targeting broadband. Each competitor illuminated a different dimension of what AST was actually selling, and what it was not.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: The Scaled Threat

No competitive development altered the landscape more than SpaceX's formal entry into non-terrestrial network connectivity. The August 2022 joint announcement between SpaceX and T-Mobile US — delivered on stage by Elon Musk and T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert at a SpaceX facility in Boca Chica — was a strategic jolt to the sector. SpaceX would embed direct-to-cell capability into its Version 2 Mini satellite constellation, using the mid-band PCS spectrum licensed by T-Mobile under a spectrum-sharing arrangement. Initial service, T-Mobile committed, would support text messaging; voice and data would follow.

SpaceX began launching Direct to Cell-capable satellites in January 2024. [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com) reported that the first operational text messaging service launched as a beta in late 2024, with T-Mobile subscribers in coverage gaps receiving SMS connectivity. By mid-2025, SpaceX had deployed hundreds of Direct to Cell-capable v2 Mini satellites alongside its broader Starlink broadband constellation, giving the program a pace of infrastructure build-out that no standalone competitor could match.

The architecture of the two systems, however, diverges in ways that matter commercially and technically. Starlink Direct to Cell relies on SpaceX's own satellite spectrum allocations — specifically T-Mobile's licensed terrestrial PCS Band 25 — shared under a bilateral arrangement, rather than integrating into each MNO partner's own licensed frequencies across dozens of national markets. The practical consequence is that SpaceX must negotiate separately with each carrier in each country, and regulatory clearance of satellite-to-mobile transmissions on terrestrial spectrum bands is a slow, country-by-country process. AST's model, by contrast, embeds AST infrastructure as a virtual extension of the partner MNO's own licensed spectrum, a legal and technical posture that has allowed agreements across more than fifty countries.

The throughput arithmetic also differs. AST's competitive claim rests on aperture. BlueWalker 3's unfurled phased array measured approximately 64.5 square metres — at launch in September 2022, the largest commercial communications array ever deployed in low-Earth orbit. BlueBird Block 1 satellites, beginning their launches in September 2024, carried arrays of ~~comparable or greater scale~~ ==comparable scale, with the next material aperture step-up reserved for the Block 2 / BlueBird 6 design==. Physics dictates that a larger aperture collects more signal and narrows the beamwidth, translating to meaningfully higher achievable data rates at the handset. Starlink Direct to Cell, integrated into the compact v2 Mini bus, operates with a significantly smaller antenna aperture. Independent link-budget analyses circulated in the satellite engineering community consistently placed AST's theoretical peak throughput per satellite above Starlink Direct to Cell's, though SpaceX's constellation density provides its own offsetting advantage through frequency reuse across many simultaneous beams.

| | **AST SpaceMobile** | **Starlink Direct to Cell** |
|---|---|---|
| Antenna aperture (operational) | Large phased array (~64 m² per satellite) | Integrated panel on v2 Mini bus (substantially smaller) |
| Spectrum model | Partner MNO's licensed terrestrial bands | SpaceX-licensed / T-Mobile Band 25 (US) |
| MNO partnerships | 50+ countries, AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, others | T-Mobile (US), bilateral international deals |
| Initial service tier | Voice, SMS, broadband data | SMS/text beta, voice and data follow-on |
| Operational milestone | BlueBird Block 1 launches Sep 2024 | Direct-to-Cell v2 Mini launches Jan 2024 |
| Ownership model | Independent listed company (NASDAQ: ASTS) | Division of privately held SpaceX |

The most structurally significant asymmetry may be financial. SpaceX's internal capital flows and lack of public-market disclosure obligations insulate Starlink Direct to Cell from the quarterly earnings scrutiny that AST faced as a listed company. SpaceX could cross-subsidise the Direct to Cell program from its broader Starlink broadband revenues. AST had no such backstop, which made the pace of its Block 2 satellite deployment and the conversion of its MNO agreements from letters of intent into revenue-generating commercial contracts the central financial narrative of its early operational years.

## Lynk Global: The Narrowband Incumbent

Lynk Global, founded in 2017 by Charles Miller and operating as a private company through the frozen snapshot, represented a different competitive posture: narrowband, low-throughput direct-to-cell connectivity aimed primarily at text messaging and IoT device management rather than broadband data services. Lynk claimed the first cellular text message sent from a satellite directly to an unmodified handset in 2020, a demonstration that established the concept before AST's BlueWalker 3 flight and before SpaceX's public entry.

Lynk's commercial agreements concentrated on smaller and emerging-market carriers — operators in Africa, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia for whom even basic text connectivity in rural dead zones was a meaningful service improvement. The architecture used much smaller satellites and accepted the throughput limitations that smaller apertures impose. For Lynk's target customers, this was sufficient: a carrier offering unmodified handset connectivity for emergency text or low-rate IoT telemetry did not need the broadband data rates that AST's large arrays were designed to deliver.

The competitive overlap with AST was therefore partial. Where AST pursued the major MNO relationships — AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Telstra, MTN — Lynk operated in segments those carriers had not prioritised. In practice, Lynk had arguably done more to validate the regulatory and commercial model than to compete directly for the same contracts. The existence of operational Lynk service, however modest in throughput, demonstrated to regulators in multiple jurisdictions that direct-to-cell satellite transmissions on terrestrial spectrum bands were technically and legally manageable — a proof of concept that eased some of the regulatory path for broader industry players.

## Apple and Globalstar: A Narrow-Band Reference Point

Apple's satellite emergency messaging feature, introduced with iPhone 14 in September 2022 and powered by Globalstar's network, occupied a distinct niche that illuminated the competitive space by contrast rather than by direct competition. The feature used Globalstar's narrowband 850 MHz spectrum and a custom antenna architecture within the iPhone to enable emergency SOS texts and crash detection alerts in areas without cellular coverage. Apple subsidised Globalstar's network investment through a long-term services agreement, providing Globalstar guaranteed revenues and providing Apple a product differentiator.

The service was explicitly limited: no voice, no broadband, emergency and location-reporting use cases only. It required antenna accommodation within Apple's own hardware, not generic handset compatibility. AST's entire proposition depended on connecting to any existing LTE-capable handset without modification — the billions of devices already in circulation globally. Apple-Globalstar demonstrated that the consumer market accepted satellite connectivity as a concept; it did not compete for the broadband and voice services that AST's architecture targeted.

## Where the Differentiation Line Holds

By the time BlueBird Block 1 satellites began launching in September 2024, the competitive map had clarified enough that AST's differentiation arguments had been tested against real alternatives rather than hypothetical ones. Three claims remained structurally durable.

First, the antenna aperture advantage was physical and not easily replicated by competitors deploying smaller satellites at mass-production economics. Higher data rates per satellite required larger arrays, and larger arrays required either larger buses or unfurling mechanisms — both costly and logistically complex.

Second, the MNO partnership model provided a geographic and commercial reach that bilateral, carrier-by-carrier spectrum deals could not replicate at speed. Fifty-plus country agreements, anchored by strategic equity holdings from Vodafone and Rakuten, meant that AST's commercial surface was distributed across mobile subscriber bases numbering in the billions.

Third, the spectrum architecture — embedding AST infrastructure within the MNO's own licensed spectrum — created a legal and regulatory alignment with host-country carriers that an independent satellite operator deploying its own spectrum had to negotiate from a weaker position in most markets.

Against these strengths, the competitive risk Starlink Direct to Cell posed was not primarily technical but executional: SpaceX's constellation-building pace, financial durability, and existing regulatory relationships with major markets gave it the capacity to close any throughput gap over time, even if the physics-per-satellite favoured AST's larger arrays. The rate at which that gap narrowed, and the rate at which AST's MNO agreements converted to operating revenues, would determine which differentiation arguments remained relevant through the Block 2 deployment cycle.

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through BlueWalker, SPAC, BlueBird launches, MNO partnerships
chapters.body:
## The Founding Thesis

Abel Avellan incorporated AST SpaceMobile in Midland, Texas in 2017 carrying a proposition that the satellite communications establishment had largely dismissed as technically intractable: that a low Earth orbit constellation could connect directly to standard, unmodified smartphones without specialist hardware. The insight was not merely engineering — it was commercial. By routing service through existing mobile network operators rather than selling directly to consumers, AST could inherit subscriber bases numbering in the billions, bypass the subscriber-acquisition cost that had broken earlier satellite ventures, and access the licensed cellular spectrum that MNO partners already held. Avellan had sold his previous satellite communications company, Emerging Markets Communications, to Global Eagle Entertainment in 2016 for approximately $550 million, and brought that operational pedigree — alongside earlier stints at Hughes Electronics and Astrolink — to what would become the most consequential direct-to-cell bet in the capital markets.

The engineering challenge the founding thesis demanded was acute. Standard handsets transmit power in the range of one-quarter of a watt. Bridging that signal across the roughly 700-kilometre gap to a LEO satellite required an antenna aperture orders of magnitude larger than anything previously flown commercially — a large, unfurled phased-array that could concentrate enough gain to close the link. That antenna became the defining technical artifact of the BlueBird programme and the central uncertainty investors would price for years.

## SPAC Listing and Early Capital Formation

AST SpaceMobile went public on April 7, 2021, through a merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp, listing on NASDAQ under the ticker ASTS. The SPAC vehicle provided the liquidity event and balance-sheet capitalisation necessary to fund a constellation programme whose hardware costs, rocket manifest, and multi-year operating losses placed it well beyond the reach of private venture structures alone. Strategic equity capital followed. ~~Vodafone, Rakuten Mobile, AT&T, and Google each took stakes in the company prior to or around the listing, a set of pre-commercial validations that carried significant signalling weight: the investors were not financial sponsors placing macro bets but MNOs and a major technology platform with direct commercial stakes in whether the direct-to-cell service worked.~~ ==Vodafone and Rakuten Mobile took stakes in the company around the 2021 listing, with AT&T and Google following through the January 2024 strategic investment. The set of pre-commercial validations carried significant signalling weight: the investors were not financial sponsors placing macro bets but MNOs and a major technology platform with direct commercial stakes in whether the direct-to-cell service worked.== Vodafone's participation in particular — a group operating across multiple European and African markets — gave the company a foothold in geographies where connectivity gaps made direct-to-cell economically most compelling.

Revenue in the public period was modest and structurally pre-commercial. Engineering services and pre-commercial partner contributions produced approximately $11 million in 2022 and ~~$12 million in 2023~~ ==zero GAAP revenue in 2023==, against substantial operating losses reflecting the cost base of a company simultaneously designing satellites, qualifying launch contracts, standing up ground infrastructure, and negotiating spectrum arrangements across dozens of national jurisdictions. The financial profile was that of a deep-capital-expenditure infrastructure build, not a software company, and the market valued it accordingly — oscillating sharply on technical milestones and competitive news rather than trailing revenue.

## BlueWalker 3: Proof of Concept in Orbit

The pivotal technical validation came on September 10, 2022, when AST SpaceMobile launched the BlueWalker 3 prototype aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral. BlueWalker 3 carried an unfurled phased-array antenna measuring approximately 693 square feet — the largest commercial communications antenna ever deployed in LEO at the time of launch. The satellite was not designed for commercial service; it was a demonstration platform to validate the link physics at scale and to generate the regulatory data needed for spectrum licensing globally.

Over the following months, the company reported a sequence of escalating test achievements. Voice calls were completed over standard commercially available handsets without any hardware modification. Data sessions were established on existing LTE bands. By early 2023, AST reported peak downlink speeds in 4G LTE testing that, while modest by terrestrial standards, demonstrated that the fundamental link closure problem — the problem that had made direct-to-cell seem implausible — had been solved at prototype scale. The BlueWalker 3 results provided the technical foundation for the commercial BlueBird design and reoriented investor perception of the programme from speculative concept to executable engineering.

## BlueBird Block 1: First Operational Satellites

AST SpaceMobile launched its first five operational BlueBird Block 1 satellites on September 12, 2024, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9. The launch marked the company's transition from pre-operational to early operational status — the moment at which the direct-to-cell network moved from prototype demonstration to commercial-grade hardware in orbit. ~~Block 1 satellites carried substantially larger phased-array apertures than BlueWalker 3, designed and qualified for operational service rather than prototype testing.~~ ==Block 1 satellites were designed and qualified for operational service rather than prototype testing, though the major aperture step-up over BlueWalker 3 is reserved for the Block 2/BlueBird 6 design rather than realised in the Block 1 platform.==

The September 2024 Block 1 deployment was followed by activation procedures and initial commercial testing with MNO partners. The company began working toward the commercial service launches that had been contractually anticipated in its MNO agreements. Revenue from commercial mobile services — which had not materialized in material form through the pre-Block 1 period, with 2024 reported revenue ~~declining to approximately $5 million~~ ==of $4.418 million== as engineering services wound down — was now the near-term operational objective. The financial trajectory from this point forward depended on the pace at which MNO partners converted the technical capability into subscriber-facing service.

## MNO Partnership Architecture

The mobile network operator partnership roster that AST SpaceMobile assembled ~~between the 2021 listing and the Block 1 launch~~ ==between the 2021 listing and the May 2026 snapshot== constituted the commercial framework through which the direct-to-cell service would monetise. In the United States, ~~multi-year agreements with both AT&T and Verizon positioned AST as a supplemental coverage layer for the two largest domestic carriers.~~ ==definitive commercial agreements with AT&T (announced May 15, 2024) and Verizon (announced October 8, 2025) positioned AST as a supplemental coverage layer for the two largest domestic carriers.== Internationally, Vodafone's strategic equity stake anchored European and African coverage. Rakuten Mobile provided the Japanese market entry. Bell Canada extended coverage northward; Telstra covered the Australian market; MTN Group addressed the African continent. By the time the Block 1 satellites were operational, the company had reached agreements covering more than fifty countries — a geographic footprint that, if commercially activated, would represent one of the largest satellite service footprints ever assembled.

The commercial logic of the partnership model was that AST would charge MNOs on a wholesale basis for connectivity capacity consumed by their subscribers, while the MNOs handled the retail customer relationship, billing, and the regulatory spectrum licenses under which the service operated. Subscribers would receive service automatically when outside terrestrial coverage — no app download, no secondary SIM, no hardware change required. The simplicity of the customer experience was a deliberate design choice, intended to make the satellite layer effectively invisible and therefore scalable at the MNO's existing subscriber base without incremental marketing cost.

## Forward Catalysts at Frozen Snapshot

As of the May 2026 frozen snapshot, the forward event sequence driving AST SpaceMobile's investment narrative centred on three interrelated catalysts. First, the Block 2 satellite programme — featuring antenna apertures estimated at two to three times the size of Block 1 designs, yielding substantially higher capacity per satellite and a more favourable per-gigabyte economics — was advancing toward deployment. The Block 2 scale-up was the principal constellation-capacity event that would determine whether the network could support material commercial traffic volumes across its MNO partner footprint.

Second, the commercial service launches with MNO partners in the United States and internationally were the revenue-conversion moment the company's entire capital structure had been built around. The transition from engineering-services revenue to subscription-linked commercial revenue would represent the first test of the monetisation model at commercial scale.

Third, additional MNO partner additions — expanding the fifty-country roster further, particularly in markets with large underserved populations and limited terrestrial infrastructure — continued to extend the total addressable market and the geographic density of the constellation utilisation case.

Capital structure adequacy was the constraint threading through all three catalysts. The constellation deployment programme was capital-intensive at a scale that required continued access to equity and debt markets through the deployment period. The strategic equity base — with ~~AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and Google all holding stakes~~ ==AT&T, Vodafone, Rakuten, and Google all holding stakes== — provided both financial and strategic support, but the multi-year deployment cadence meant that capital requirements extended well beyond the Block 1 milestone. How management navigated the capital stack through the Block 2 programme would determine whether the commercial service launch could be executed at the scale the MNO agreements contemplated.

chapters.title: Phased-array antenna, direct-to-cell engineering, and patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Aperture Problem and How Avellan Solved It

The engineering challenge at the heart of AST SpaceMobile's business is a physics problem that had defeated every previous attempt at satellite-to-handset connectivity: how to close a broadband communications link between a satellite 550 kilometres overhead and a smartphone designed to talk to a cell tower three kilometres away. The signal path is roughly two hundred times longer. The handset's antenna gain does not change. The satellite must compensate.

Every direct-to-cell predecessor accepted that constraint as a ceiling. The result was either narrowband messaging services or hardware-modified devices—approaches that required either truncated utility or MNO cooperation in distributing proprietary handsets. AST SpaceMobile's founders chose a third path: push the physics in the direction of aperture.

Abel Avellan and his chief scientist filed the company's first patent claims in 2017, the year they established the company in Midland, Texas. The foundational insight was that a sufficiently large phased-array antenna—deployed in low Earth orbit, driven by purpose-built digital signal processing—could generate enough effective isotropic radiated power to close a wideband 4G LTE link with a standard commercial handset. The phased array acts simultaneously as a spatially directed transmitter and a steerable receiver, electronically forming and moving beams across the coverage footprint without any mechanical articulation. The larger the aperture, the greater the antenna gain, and the more gain available to trade against the distance penalty of the orbital geometry.

## BlueWalker 3: Demonstrating the Principle at Scale

The physical ambition of that wager became visible to the world on 10 November 2022, when the BlueWalker 3 prototype completed its antenna deployment in orbit. The array spanned [693 square feet—64.4 square metres](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220908005651/en/AST-SpaceMobile-Announces-BlueWalker-3-the-Largest-Commercial-Communications-Array-Ever-Deployed-to-Low-Earth-Orbit)—making it the largest commercial communications array ever deployed to low Earth orbit. It had been stowed during the September 2022 Falcon 9 launch inside a volume little larger than an industrial refrigerator. Once on orbit, 148-micron panels unfolded autonomously, generating solar power on the Sun-facing side and transmitting and receiving cellular signals through the antenna elements facing Earth.

BlueWalker 3's link budget performance validated internal projections and materially de-risked the full BlueBird production commitment that followed. The satellite completed voice calls over standard LTE on unmodified smartphones and by April 2023 demonstrated 5G connectivity at data rates sufficient for video streaming. The prototype also surfaced an unintended consequence: BlueWalker 3 appeared among the fifty brightest objects in the night sky under certain solar angles, generating a [study published in *Nature*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06672-7) that influenced AST's optical reflectivity mitigation approach for subsequent generations.

## The Doppler and Interference Problems

Operating in standard cellular bands from a platform moving at approximately 7.5 kilometres per second introduces two intertwined engineering problems that do not arise in geostationary satellite communications. At 2 GHz, orbital velocity produces a peak frequency offset of roughly ±50 kHz—beyond the tolerance of an unmodified LTE or 5G modem without correction. AST's approach, codified across its patent families and later aligned with 3GPP Release 17 and 18 NR-NTN specifications, places the Doppler pre-correction burden entirely on the satellite. The payload computes and applies a frequency offset that anticipates the shift each handset will experience, so that by the time the signal arrives at the phone, it falls within the modem's acceptable error window. The satellite's digital signal processor must execute this calculation continuously and independently for every simultaneous user beam.

The second constraint is terrestrial interference. AST SpaceMobile shares spectrum with its MNO partners—the same low-band and mid-band frequencies used by AT&T's 850 MHz network in the United States, Verizon's equivalent bands, and Vodafone's European allocations. A satellite beam with an uncontrolled footprint risks interfering with cell towers below in high-density areas. The company's beam-steering algorithms form tight spot beams so that each illuminates only the geographic zone where service is needed: where terrestrial coverage is dense, beams are withheld; where a user sits in a coverage gap, the beam is precisely directed. The patent literature describes configurations supporting hundreds of discrete simultaneous cells per satellite.

## The AST5000 ASIC: Proprietary Silicon as Structural Moat

Processing ten gigahertz of phased-array bandwidth in real time—while simultaneously executing beam steering, Doppler pre-compensation, and handover logic for thousands of users—cannot be accomplished with commercial off-the-shelf electronics rated for the radiation environment of LEO. AST SpaceMobile spent an estimated [$45 million and approximately 150 engineer-years](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240327367837/en/AST-SpaceMobile-ASIC-Chip-Enters-Tape-Out-Phase-in-Collaboration-with-TSMC) developing the AST5000, a proprietary application-specific integrated circuit that entered tape-out at TSMC in March 2024, designed in collaboration with Cadence's electronic design automation platform. The chip supports 10 GHz of processing bandwidth and enables each Block 2 satellite to manage more than 2,000 simultaneous coverage cells at peak data speeds of 120 Mbps per cell.

Because the AST5000 is proprietary and radiation-hardened for the LEO environment, any competitor seeking to replicate the full system architecture would face a multi-year silicon development programme of comparable cost and duration before reaching production. This structural feature converts what might otherwise be a temporarily defensible engineering lead into a more durable barrier: ramping a novel ASIC from concept to production takes years even for well-capitalised organisations. Avellan has been direct about what this manufacturing achievement represents:

> "Simply put, we are the first company in the history of commercial satellite manufacturing to produce satellites of our size and power at scale."

## The Patent Portfolio: Scope and Competitive Signal

AST SpaceMobile's patent programme began with those 2017 filings by Avellan and his chief scientist. The portfolio reached its 1,000th claim by [March 2021](https://ast-science.com/ast-and-science-announces-1000th-patent-claim/), a milestone the company publicly marked. The pace of filings accelerated through the BlueBird development cycle: by early 2024, total claims exceeded 3,100; by the [FY 2024 10-K filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1780312/000095017025030909/asts-20241231.htm), the portfolio stood at more than 3,500 patent and patent-pending claims across 36 patent families worldwide, with approximately 1,050 officially granted or allowed as of mid-2024. Avellan is personally listed as co-inventor on 24 U.S. patents.

The most cited patent in the portfolio is [US9973266B1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9973266B1/ko), "System and method for high throughput fractionated satellites (HTFS) for direct connectivity to and from end user devices and terminals using flight formations of small or very small satellites," which has received 96 forward citations from companies including Lynk Global and UbiquitiLink—direct competitors in the emerging direct-to-device sector. That citation pattern is diagnostic: the foundational architecture Avellan established has become the reference point against which later entrants must design around.

The 36 patent families span phased-array antenna design, large deployable structures, beam-forming and beam-steering algorithms, Doppler compensation methods, satellite-to-handset link-budget techniques, constellation management, interference coordination with terrestrial networks, and the satellite manufacturing processes required to fold, deploy, and verify arrays at production scale rather than in a prototype context.

## Block 2 and the Accumulating Aperture Advantage

BlueBird 6, the first Block 2 satellite, launched in December 2025 aboard an Indian LVM-3 rocket and [completed array unfolding in February 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260210108166/en/AST-SpaceMobile-Successfully-Completes-Unfolding-of-BlueBird-6-the-Largest-Commercial-Communications-Array-Antenna-Ever-Deployed-in-Low-Earth-Orbit), deploying approximately 2,400 square feet of phased array—more than three times larger than the Block 1 arrays, and the third time in the company's history it had claimed the record for the largest commercial communications array in low Earth orbit. ~~The successive aperture expansions from BlueWalker 3 to Block 1 to Block 2 reflect the systematic application of folding-mechanism patents, panel manufacturing processes, and deployment dynamics documented and protected across the portfolio.~~ ==The Block 1 satellites carried arrays of broadly the same scale as the BlueWalker 3 prototype, with the major aperture step-up arriving in the Block 2/BlueBird 6 design. That step-up reflects the systematic application of folding-mechanism patents, panel manufacturing processes, and deployment dynamics documented and protected across the portfolio.==

Avellan has been consistent about the competitive consequence:

> "We are the only company capable of delivering 4G and 5G and in the future, 6G broadband speed sufficient for voice calls, voice over LTE, live video calls, streaming, and full Internet access directly to unmodified devices."

Whether that exclusivity holds as 3GPP Release 18 and 19 NR-NTN standards make the underlying technical specifications more widely legible is one of the central questions in the sector. What the patent estate, the AST5000 ASIC, and the cumulative manufacturing learning curve collectively represent—as of the May 2026 snapshot—is a multi-year head start in a capital-intensive, physics-constrained discipline where catching up requires not just money but time.

chapters.title: Block 2 execution, Starlink competition, capital structure, regulatory
chapters.body:
## Block 2 Deployment Execution

The five BlueBird Block 1 satellites launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 on September 12, 2024 demonstrated that AST SpaceMobile's large-aperture phased-array architecture could deliver voice and broadband data directly to unmodified handsets at commercial grade. But five satellites constitute a demonstration constellation, not a commercial network. The burden of proof for AST SpaceMobile's long-term value thesis rests on Block 2: a generation of substantially larger spacecraft — carrying roughly two to three times the antenna aperture of Block 1 — that the company has targeted for deployment through 2025 and 2026.

The execution risks are layered. Block 2 satellites represent a meaningful step-change in satellite mass and complexity; manufacturing throughput at scale has historically been the single most common failure mode for novel LEO operators. AST's satellite production relies on a relatively small industrial base at its Midland, Texas facility and on component supply chains that include precision RF hardware. Any sustained bottleneck — whether in antenna assembly, phased-array electronics, or integration testing — would lengthen the gap between Block 1's proof-of-concept posture and the minimum-viable commercial footprint needed to serve AT&T, Verizon, and Vodafone subscribers at meaningful scale. The company has not disclosed a per-satellite manufacturing cost floor for Block 2, which limits external scrutiny of whether the unit economics pencil at the targeted capacity levels.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: Competitive Pressure from a Vertically Integrated Rival

SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell program, developed through a T-Mobile partnership, represents the sharpest competitive pressure AST SpaceMobile faces. Starlink began rolling out direct-to-handset SMS capability in beta in late 2024, using v2 Mini satellites that carry a dedicated cellular payload operating on T-Mobile's licensed spectrum. The asymmetry between the two approaches is stark: SpaceX can manufacture and launch hundreds of satellites per year on its own rockets at costs that remain proprietary and almost certainly below market rates, and it can subsidise Direct to Cell cross-functionally within a company whose launch revenue and Starlink broadband subscription base dwarf AST's capitalization.

SpaceX's architecture differs materially. Starlink DTC uses a relatively small antenna per satellite but compensates through constellation density and the ability to continuously refresh orbital planes. AST argues that the large-aperture design of BlueBird delivers meaningfully better link budget — and therefore higher data throughput to the handset — than smaller-antenna competitors. The counterargument from the market is straightforward: if Starlink DTC achieves "good enough" coverage for text and low-data-rate connectivity at effectively zero incremental cost to T-Mobile subscribers, the commercial case for MNOs to pay AST for a premium direct-to-cell tier becomes harder to make. The competitive dynamic is further complicated by the fact that SpaceX remains AST's primary launch provider, creating a degree of dependency on a direct rival that has no structural parallel in the satellite industry.

## Capital Structure Adequacy Through Full Constellation

AST SpaceMobile's financial position through the end of ~~2024~~ ==2025== reflected the realities of a pre-commercial hardware program. ~~Engineering-services revenue — roughly $11 million in 2022, $12 million in 2023, and falling to approximately $5 million in 2024 as billable development milestones wound down — covered only a fraction of operating expenditure.~~ ==GAAP revenue — zero in 2023, $4.418 million in 2024, and $70.918 million in 2025 as gateway equipment sales and early service and government contributions began to materialise — covered only a fraction of operating expenditure.== The company has financed constellation deployment through a combination of strategic equity from Vodafone, Rakuten Mobile, AT&T, and Google, as well as post-SPAC equity raises and convertible debt instruments.

The adequacy question sharpens as Block 2 spending ramps. A full commercial constellation capable of continuous coverage across the 50-plus countries where AST holds MNO agreements would require dozens of Block 2 satellites; the capital intensity of that deployment, set against a revenue ramp that remains in its earliest innings, creates a funding gap that equity markets and existing partners must bridge. Equity dilution at current valuations is expensive; convertible instruments carry reset provisions and interest loads that accumulate during any deployment delay. Management has not provided a fully itemized total constellation cost figure in SEC filings, which leaves analysts modelling a range of scenarios. Investors who underwrote AST at its SPAC listing at an assumed target price must tolerate a longer-than-expected path to cash generation if Block 2 slips even modestly against schedule.

## Regulatory and Spectrum Coordination

AST SpaceMobile's architecture turns on a distinctive regulatory posture: rather than seeking its own global spectrum licences, it operates on spectrum already licensed to its MNO partners in each territory. This avoids the multi-decade ITU coordination battles that shaped legacy GEO satellite operators and the secondary market that has historically extracted rent from spectrum-scarce new entrants. On paper, it is an elegant solution. In practice, it disaggregates the regulatory problem into dozens of national approval processes, each requiring a regulator to sanction a space station transmitting on terrestrially-allocated bands in its jurisdiction.

Several major markets — including Japan, where Rakuten Mobile is an equity partner — have required bespoke regulatory filings and extended coordination periods. In-orbit frequency coordination with adjacent LEO constellations, particularly Starlink, adds a further dimension: the ITU coordination procedures for non-geostationary orbit systems are notoriously slow, and as the low-Earth orbit environment becomes more congested, interference avoidance agreements become harder to negotiate bilaterally. Any material regulatory delay in a Tier 1 market — the United States, Europe, India, Japan — compresses the near-term addressable revenue and undermines the "global coverage" story that underpins the MNO commercial pitches.

## MNO Partnership Commercial Conversion

AST SpaceMobile has assembled what is by any measure an impressive pre-commercial partner roster: AT&T and Verizon in the United States, Vodafone across multiple European and African markets, Rakuten Mobile in Japan, Bell Canada, Telstra in Australia, MTN across sub-Saharan Africa, and additional operators extending coverage to more than fifty countries in aggregate. The strategic and equity investment from several of these partners lends the agreements credibility that pure letter-of-intent relationships lack.

The conversion risk is nonetheless real. MNO agreements at this stage are typically structured around commercial milestones — minimum coverage thresholds, service-level commitments, pricing floors — that AST must hit before recurring per-subscriber or capacity revenue flows. An MNO operating under competitive pressure from fixed-wireless access, rival satellite entrants, or domestic spectrum auctions may elect to renegotiate terms, delay rollout, or, in an extreme case, substitute a competing direct-to-cell provider if the competitive landscape shifts. ~~The revenue trajectory through 2024 — declining rather than growing as engineering services completed — illustrates how quickly the financial profile changes when milestone-based contributions end and subscriber-based revenue has not yet begun.~~ ==The revenue trajectory into 2025 — a step up to $70.918 million but still small against the constellation-scale spend base — illustrates how far the financial profile still has to travel before recurring subscriber-based revenue reaches the run-rate needed to cover ongoing operating expenditure.==

## Launch Service Availability and Cost

AST SpaceMobile's Block 1 deployment was executed entirely on SpaceX Falcon 9. The relationship has been productive but structurally uncomfortable: SpaceX's own Starlink DTC is a direct competitive product, and launch manifest access is ultimately allocated at SpaceX's commercial discretion. Falcon 9 pricing for dedicated rideshare is public and competitive, but dedicated large-batch manifests for a customer with a competing satellite service could, in principle, be deprioritised relative to Starlink's own internal launches.

AST has not publicly disclosed binding launch agreements for the full Block 2 constellation. Alternative launch providers — United Launch Alliance's Vulcan, Rocket Lab's Neutron (still in development as of mid-2026), and Arianespace — each carry either payload capacity constraints or uncertain pricing relative to Falcon 9. A meaningful delay in securing launch slots, or a step-up in launch cost per kilogramme, flows directly into the capital adequacy calculus above. The interdependence between deployment schedule, launch cost, and funding runway means that any adverse development in one variable propagates quickly through the others, compressing the margin for execution error that a pre-revenue company can absorb.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Deployment Inflection

From the vantage point of late May 2026, AST SpaceMobile occupies an unusual position in the satellite-to-cellular universe: it has crossed the threshold from pre-operational into early commercial without yet generating the revenue profile that would justify its market capitalisation on conventional multiples. The five BlueBird Block 1 satellites launched in September 2024 demonstrated commercial-grade direct-to-cell capability, but five satellites — covering roughly 15 percent of any given orbital pass — offer sporadic rather than continuous coverage. The story of the next twelve months is Block 2 deployment, and everything that flows from it.

Block 2's substantially larger antenna surface area — approximately two to three times that of Block 1 — translates into higher equivalent isotropic radiated power per satellite, lower path loss, and the ability to serve denser populations with meaningful throughput. The operative question heading into mid-2026 is not whether the technology works — BlueWalker 3 and Block 1 have settled that debate in AST's favour — but whether the manufacturing cadence, launch schedule, and network operations scale fast enough to convert the MNO partnership book into billings before the capital structure requires further equity dilution.

## Quarter-by-Quarter Catalyst Calendar

The next four quarters present a reasonably well-defined catalyst sequence, anchored by earnings prints, launch windows, and several binary programme milestones.

**Q2 2026 (reporting approximately August 2026).** The quarterly earnings will be ~~the first to include a full quarter of whatever commercial service revenue AT&T and Verizon have begun billing their customers for SpaceMobile coverage~~ ==scrutinised for the first signs of AT&T or Verizon commercial billing, given that the Q1 2026 10-Q still described SpaceMobile Service as pending limited, noncontinuous initiation rather than already underway==. Analyst attention will focus on the revenue recognised versus the deferred revenue balance — a rising deferred figure suggests MNO partners are activating service agreements but that ASTS has not yet satisfied the performance obligations for revenue recognition. The Block 2 cumulative on-orbit count will be disclosed; each additional satellite materially expands geographic footprint and peak-simultaneous-user capacity.

**Q3 2026 (reporting approximately November 2026).** By Q3, a sufficiently large constellation — assuming on-plan deployment — should support the first meaningful broadband data revenue alongside voice and SMS. International MNO partners, particularly Vodafone's European footprint and Rakuten in Japan, could begin activating commercial service. The Q3 print will also update the cash and equivalents balance: the pace of burn relative to the capital raise runway is the solvency gating metric. Any secondary offering or convertible issuance would likely be announced in this window if the balance sheet requires reinforcement.

**Q4 2026 (reporting approximately February–March 2027).** Year-end earnings anchor the full-year 2026 revenue figure against which analyst models will assess whether the commercial ramp is tracking ==the company's $150–200 million guidance and== consensus or lagging. More significantly, management will provide FY 2027 guidance — the single most important data point in the forward dossier. If Avellan can frame 2027 with confidence, citing contracted MNO billing commitments and coverage targets, it would materially change the valuation discussion.

**Q1 2027 (reporting approximately May 2027).** The first quarter of what consensus models assume to be the material commercial scale year. Revenue will need to show sequential acceleration to validate the FY 2027 thesis; Q1 seasonality in most mobile markets is the softest demand period and must be separated from structural trend.

## Consensus Estimates and Implied Growth

ASTS's revenue profile through 2025 was dominated by engineering services fees and pre-commercial partner contributions. The commercial service inflection is expected to produce a step-change in the forward revenue line.

| Period | Revenue estimate (consensus range) | Y/Y growth | Adj. EPS |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2025A | ~~$20–45M~~ ==~$71M (actual)== | — | Deep negative |
| Q2 2026E | ~~$25–60M~~ ==~$30–50M== | — | Negative |
| Q3 2026E | ~~$60–130M~~ ==~$40–60M== | — | Negative |
| Q4 2026E | ~~$110–220M~~ ==~$50–75M== | — | Narrowing |
| FY 2026E | ~~$220–550M~~ ==~$150–200M (company guidance)== | ~~+400%+ vs. 2025E~~ ==~115–180% vs. 2025A== | Negative |
| FY 2027E | ~$700M–$1.5B+ | ~~3–4× vs. 2026E~~ ==~3.5–7× vs. 2026E== | Breakeven approach |

Ranges are wide because sell-side coverage of ASTS shows substantial dispersion reflecting genuine uncertainty in deployment cadence and MNO billing activation timing. The implied FY 2026-to-2027 growth rate in the bull case is exceptional: if the Block 2 constellation reaches the threshold satellite count for meaningful continuous US coverage before year-end 2026 and AT&T and Verizon activate billing at scale, the revenue ramp could be genuinely hyperbolic. The bear case sees deployment delays pushing material commercial revenue into 2027 and beyond.

## Management Guidance

~~Avellan has consistently avoided providing hard revenue guidance, citing dependency on launch manifest and regulatory timelines. He has framed the commercial trajectory in terms of satellite deployment milestones rather than financial metrics:~~ ==Management has issued full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $150 million to $200 million, framed against the launch manifest, regulatory timelines, and MNO billing activation pace. Avellan has paired the numeric range with operational language about satellite deployment milestones:==

> "Every satellite we launch increases our addressable service area and the number of subscribers we can serve simultaneously. The economics are fundamentally different from traditional satellite businesses because our revenue scales with the MNO billing relationships, not with direct subscriber acquisition costs."

On the competitive position relative to Starlink Direct to Cell:

> "We are operating on licensed spectrum provided by our MNO partners. We appear to those handsets as a normal cellular tower. There is no app to download, no new SIM card, no new device. That is the fundamental commercial differentiator."

The company's public disclosures have emphasised cumulative satellite count, antenna area deployed, and covered population ~~over revenue guidance — a framework that communicates operational progress without committing to a revenue recognition timeline dependent on MNO billing system integrations~~ ==alongside the $150–200 million FY 2026 revenue range, which itself carries an explicit dependency on MNO billing system integrations==.

## Metrics to Watch

Four data series will determine whether the next twelve months confirms or breaks the ASTS thesis.

**Satellite count and operational status.** The raw on-orbit count matters less than the count of satellites in active commercial service. Investors should track: total launched, total commissioned, total in commercial service, and average availability. A widening gap between launched and commercial-service numbers flags integration or operational issues.

**Revenue mix shift.** The transition from partner engineering fees to commercial service revenue is the fundamental sign of activation. A quarterly print where commercial service revenue exceeds engineering services revenue for the first time would be a binary milestone the market will price explicitly.

**Cash and equivalents versus quarterly burn.** ASTS has required multiple capital raises to fund the deployment programme. Remaining runway divided by trailing quarterly cash burn provides an approximate time-to-solvency-event metric that directly affects shareholder dilution risk.

**MNO activation geography.** The number of country-markets in active commercial service, and the subscriber populations those partners cover, is the demand-side indicator. Vodafone's European activation, Rakuten's Japan activation, and the AT&T/Verizon US coverage footprint are the three largest near-term milestones.

## Beat versus Miss

Against current expectations, a beat requires: commercial service revenue in Q2 or Q3 2026 that materially exceeds the low end of the analyst range ==and tracks toward the upper bound of the $150–200 million FY guidance==; a Block 2 on-orbit count tracking ahead of the deployment schedule implied by the current launch manifest; and any early indication that MNO partners are seeing subscriber engagement that supports the contracted billing commitments.

A miss would be signalled by: commercial service revenue materially below expectations in the first commercial-scale quarters ==or a downward revision to the $150–200 million FY 2026 range==; a Block 2 delay that pushes continuous US coverage into 2027; deterioration in the cash runway implying a dilutive raise before operating cash flow can support the balance sheet; or any indication that MNO partners are renegotiating commercial terms or deferring billing activation. The earnings call transcript itself is the primary document: Avellan's language around "commercial activation" and "MNO billing" will be parsed intensely for any hedging absent from prior calls.

## The Bull and Bear Setup

The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot date is pronounced in both directions.

The bull case rests on the proposition that the hard engineering problems are solved — BlueWalker 3 and Block 1 demonstrated direct-to-cell at commercial specification — and that the next twelve months are execution and scaling rather than technology risk. If Block 2 deployment tracks to plan and the global MNO portfolio activates, AST SpaceMobile would be the only public company operating a commercial direct-to-cell satellite network at planetary scale. The addressable market — connecting roughly four billion people outside reliable terrestrial cellular coverage — is vast, and the wholesale MNO partnership model means ASTS captures a revenue share without direct subscriber acquisition costs. In the bull scenario, FY 2027 revenue of $1B or above is credible.

The bear case is structural. The capital intensity of building a LEO constellation to commercial scale is substantial. Every quarter of deployment delay extends the pre-commercial burn period. SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell programme operates on a fundamentally different cost structure, with manufacturing advantages ASTS cannot easily replicate. If competitive dynamics from Starlink constrain the ARPU that MNO partners will pay for wholesale satellite capacity, the revenue economics could land materially below consensus ==and force a downward revision to the $150–200 million FY 2026 range==. A significant secondary offering at below-market pricing would compound the dilution impact on existing shareholders.

The twelve months ahead will not leave the thesis in ambiguity. By Q1 2027, the market will have four quarters of commercial-era earnings data, a full picture of Block 2 deployment progress, and management's first credible FY 2027 guidance. The gap between bull and bear narrows materially — in one direction or the other.

chapters.title: Block 2 deployment, commercial revenue conversion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Block 2 Inflection

By the time AST SpaceMobile's initial five BlueBird Block 1 satellites had completed their on-orbit commissioning in late 2024, Abel Avellan was already defining the next phase of the company's build-out in terms that left little room for ambiguity. Block 2 was not an incremental upgrade — it was the architecture that would make direct-to-cell economics work at scale.

The design distinction was fundamental. Where Block 1 satellites carried phased-array apertures sufficient to demonstrate commercial-grade service, Block 2 buses were engineered with antenna arrays roughly two to three times the surface area, a step change in effective radiated power that translated directly into higher per-satellite throughput. Greater aperture meant the ability to serve more simultaneous users per satellite pass, to support broader spectrum allocations across partner bands, and to begin approaching the capacity density that commercial revenue models demanded. The company framed Block 2 in regulatory filings and investor communications not as a further technical proof of concept but as the backbone of a financially self-sustaining network — the first generation whose economics could plausibly close.

[AST SpaceMobile investor relations](https://investors.ast-science.com) filings through 2024 indicated Block 2 satellite manufacturing was underway in Midland, Texas, with launches intended to begin in 2025 and extend through 2026. The deployment arc envisioned multiple missions on SpaceX Falcon 9 vehicles, building toward a constellation sufficient for initial commercial coverage across priority equatorial and mid-latitude markets — geographies that account for the overwhelming majority of the company's contracted mobile network operator subscriber base.

## MNO Revenue Conversion Mechanics

The structural logic of AST SpaceMobile's commercial model depended on a straightforward but operationally demanding sequence: launch satellites, achieve coverage, enable MNO partners to activate subscribers, and collect a revenue share. The partnership framework, as disclosed in commercial agreements with AT&T and Verizon in the United States, Vodafone across multiple European and African markets, and Rakuten in Japan, was built around wholesale arrangements in which the satellite operator would provide capacity to the MNO, with the carrier handling customer billing, plan packaging, and regulatory compliance in each jurisdiction.

AT&T's multi-year agreement, announced in ~~2023~~ ==May 2024== and extended following the Block 1 launches, provided AST SpaceMobile with a guaranteed revenue pathway into the largest subscriber market in the United States. Verizon followed with its own ~~commercial agreement, meaning the two largest US carriers by subscriber count were contracted counterparties before the first operational satellite had reached orbit~~ ==definitive commercial agreement on October 8, 2025 — roughly a year after the first Block 1 satellites had reached orbit — bringing both of the two largest US carriers by subscriber count into the contracted partner base==. Vodafone's position as both strategic investor and multi-country MNO partner gave the company a vehicle for simultaneous commercial launch across several dozen markets once adequate satellite coverage was established.

The revenue conversion challenge was not contractual but geometric. A single Block 1 satellite provided coverage over a given geographic footprint for only a fraction of each orbit, and five satellites could serve any given region for only minutes per day. Meaningful commercial revenue — beyond the engineering services and pre-commercial partner contributions that produced the modest ~~$11 million and $12 million revenues recorded in 2022 and 2023 respectively~~ ==$11 million in reported 2022 revenue, followed by zero GAAP revenue in 2023== — required a constellation large enough to provide acceptable service continuity to paying subscribers. The 2024 revenue figure of approximately $5 million reflected that the company remained in a transitional state: Block 1 satellites were in orbit and generating operational data but not yet configured for commercial billing at scale.

Block 2 deployment was therefore the linchpin of revenue conversion. Avellan, across multiple earnings call appearances through 2024, described the path to material commercial revenue as a function of constellation scale rather than any further contractual or technical uncertainty. The MNO partnerships were signed. The spectrum had been secured in most priority markets. The engineering proposition had been validated by BlueWalker 3 in 2022 and confirmed by Block 1 on-orbit operations in late 2024. What remained was putting enough satellites in orbit to generate the coverage minutes that would convert contracted agreements into cash receipts.

## Capital Structure and the 2025–2026 Funding Bridge

Scaling from five satellites to a commercially adequate constellation required capital of an order the company had not previously raised in a single cycle. Through 2024 and into 2025, AST SpaceMobile undertook a series of equity and convertible instrument transactions supported by its strategic partners. AT&T and Google made direct equity investments ==as part of the January 2024 strategic investment round==, providing both capital and a form of commercial endorsement that supported the company's ability to access institutional equity markets at acceptable terms. The combined transactions extended the company's cash runway through the anticipated Block 2 launch window.

The capital structure entering the Block 2 deployment phase carried meaningful dilution from the April 2021 SPAC merger and subsequent equity raises, but the investor base had consolidated around a set of strategic holders with long-duration interests in the commercial outcome. Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, and Google collectively held positions that aligned their incentives with execution rather than near-term financial exit. Convertible debt instruments introduced refinancing risk in the 2026–2027 window, a factor that sell-side analysts flagged as a potential source of additional dilution if constellation deployment timelines extended beyond guidance.

## Starlink Direct to Cell: The Competitive Constraint

The competitive landscape entering the Block 2 deployment window was materially different from the one Avellan had described at the company's 2021 listing. SpaceX's Starlink Direct to Cell program, executed in partnership with T-Mobile in the United States, had reached commercial service availability by 2025, placing a well-capitalised, vertically integrated competitor in the market ahead of AST SpaceMobile's own revenue ramp.

The two architectures were, however, not identical in their commercial positioning. Starlink's direct-to-cell service was built on a proprietary constellation serving a single carrier partner per major market, with SpaceX retaining control of the satellite infrastructure end-to-end. AST SpaceMobile's model was predicated on carrier-agnostic infrastructure designed to serve multiple MNOs simultaneously — a differentiation that, if it held at commercial scale, would allow the company to aggregate subscribers across AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, and more than fifty partner operators globally without replicating capital investment for each bilateral relationship.

Whether that differentiation proved commercially meaningful would ultimately depend on which architecture delivered superior coverage quality and subscriber economics at equivalent constellation sizes. The competitive pressure from Starlink DTC created urgency around Block 2 timeline execution. A prolonged deployment delay risked allowing T-Mobile to entrench an early-mover advantage with subscribers who — given the commodity nature of supplemental satellite coverage — might show limited inclination to switch providers once a service habit was established.

## 2026–2030: The Scaling Horizon

The five-year arc from 2026 through 2030 represented, in compressed form, the company's entire commercial thesis. A constellation adequate for initial commercial service — likely requiring several dozen Block 2 satellites in addition to the five Block 1 vehicles — was the minimum condition for material revenue recognition. A full global coverage build-out of the scale envisioned in FCC filings, eventually extending to several hundred satellites, was the precondition for the wholesale capacity model to generate operating leverage.

| Milestone | Constellation Scale | Commercial Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Block 2 initial deployment | ~20–30 satellites | Coverage continuity for first commercial billing wave |
| Phase I completion | ~90+ satellites | Adequate equatorial and tropical commercial coverage |
| Phase II build-out | ~168+ satellites | Expanded mid-latitude coverage; US service continuity |
| Full global constellation | 240+ satellites | Near-global MNO revenue at scale |

The financial model embedded in analyst projections through 2024 anticipated a steep revenue ramp beginning in 2025–2026 as Block 2 satellites became operational, with the company potentially approaching operating break-even sometime in the 2027–2028 window under base-case assumptions — assumptions that required no significant launch failures, no material deterioration in MNO partner commitments, and a capital markets environment that would support at least one further equity raise if deployment timelines slipped.

For Avellan, who had founded the company in Midland, Texas in 2017 with the explicit thesis that existing unmodified smartphones were already radio-compatible with a sufficiently large low-orbit phased array, the 2026–2030 horizon was not speculative territory. It was the execution phase of an engineering proposition that BlueWalker 3 had validated in September 2022 and Block 1 had confirmed in the autumn of 2024. Whether the commercial build-out could proceed at the pace the capital structure required — and far enough ahead of a Starlink Direct to Cell competitor with substantially deeper resources — remained the central, unresolved question facing the company at the frozen snapshot date.

## C. Technology Glossary

**BlueBird** — AST SpaceMobile's operational satellite series. Block 1 comprises the first five commercial-grade spacecraft. Block 2 satellites carry substantially larger phased-array antennas for higher per-satellite throughput.

financials.key_finding: AST SpaceMobile is pre-commercial-revenue. The April 2021 SPAC merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp listed the company on NASDAQ. The September 2024 BlueBird Block 1 launches (first 5 operational satellites) transitioned the company from pre-operational to early operational. The MNO partnership commercial revenue conversion plus the Block 2 deployment scaling are the principal forward strategic events.
structural_observations: Revenue is principally engineering services and pre-commercial partner contributions; commercial mobile service revenue has not begun materially.
Substantial operating losses reflecting pre-commercial constellation build-out.
Capital raises: post-SPAC equity plus subsequent equity and convertible debt instruments to fund constellation deployment.
Strategic equity partners include Vodafone, Rakuten, AT&T, Google — substantial pre-commercial validation.
BlueBird Block 1 (first 5 satellites launched September 12 2024 via SpaceX Falcon 9) demonstrated commercial-grade direct-to-cell capability.
Block 2 satellite design is substantially larger (~2-3x antenna area) targeting higher capacity per satellite; deployment scaling through 2025-2026.

leadership.key_finding: AST SpaceMobile is structurally founder Abel Avellan's company. Avellan serves as Chairman of the Board, Chief Executive Officer, and President — a triple-role structure that signals concentrated founder operational control through the multi-year capital-intensive constellation deployment programme. CFO Andrew Johnson and Chief Strategy Officer Sean Wallace plus the broader executive team support Avellan's leadership. The board includes representatives from major strategic investors (AT&T, Rakuten, Vodafone, Verizon plus the SPAC-era directors) reflecting the company's strategic partnership architecture with the major global mobile network operators.

ceo_chairman_president.framing: Avellan founded AST SpaceMobile in 2017 with the founding thesis that direct-to-cell satellite connectivity could become a meaningful commercial service through a low Earth orbit constellation designed to provide cellular broadband directly to standard unmodified mobile phones. The Venezuelan-born telecommunications industry veteran brought multi-decade satellite communications operational experience including the previous successful entrepreneurship at EMC (which sold to Global Eagle Entertainment in 2016) plus broader Hughes Electronics and Astrolink pedigree. The triple-role structure (Chairman + CEO + President) signals concentrated founder control; the continued continuity from founding through the 2021 SPAC listing and into the post-public period has been the structural anchor of the company's strategic direction. Avellan's substantial equity ownership plus the institutional shareholder structure (with strategic mobile network operator equity participation) supports continued operational and governance leadership through the multi-year deployment programme.

leadership.board_composition_observation: AST SpaceMobile's board pairs founder Chairman/CEO/President Abel Avellan with directors representing the major strategic mobile network operator investors (AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten) plus additional independent directors. The composition reflects the company's strategic partnership architecture — the direct-to-cell service depends on mobile network operator partnerships for both the spectrum access (the MNO partners provide the cellular spectrum the satellites use to provide service to MNO customers) and the customer monetisation. The MNO board representation aligns governance with these strategic relationships and provides ongoing communication channels at the senior level. The forward governance trajectory through the constellation deployment and commercial scaling depends on continued Avellan operational leadership plus the broader board composition's support of the multi-year strategic execution.
